SET 10 / EXERCISE 01

Exercise 01 — Throwing Away Data Without Losing Any Information

Domain: Sufficient statistics · Rao–Blackwell theorem · Minimum-variance unbiased estimation

Core intuition: A carefully constructed statistic can retain all information relevant to an unknown parameter while discarding irrelevant details of the original dataset.

Scenario

A research laboratory evaluates a binary classification system.

Each experiment records whether a prediction was correct or incorrect.

The team has collected thousands of binary observations and wants to estimate the model's true probability of producing a correct prediction.

A researcher proposes using the first observation as an estimator.

Another researcher argues that the entire dataset should be summarized through its total number of successes.

You are asked to investigate whether summarizing the data can actually improve the estimator without losing information about the unknown probability.

Technical setup

Let:

\[ X_1,\ldots,X_n\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p). \]

The unknown parameter is:

\[ p=P(X_i=1). \]

Consider the initial estimator:

\[ \hat p_0=X_1. \]

Define the sufficient statistic:

\[ T=\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i. \]

The Rao–Blackwellized estimator is:

\[ \hat p_{\mathrm{RB}}=\mathbb E[\hat p_0\mid T]. \]

Research challenges

  1. Derive the likelihood of the complete dataset and factor it into a parameter-dependent term and a parameter-independent term.
  2. Use the factorization theorem to establish whether (T) is sufficient for (p).
  3. Determine the conditional distribution of (X_1) given (T=t).
  4. Derive:

\[ \mathbb E[X_1\mid T]=\frac{T}{n}. \]

  1. Calculate the variance of the original estimator:

\[ \operatorname{Var}(\hat p_0). \]

  1. Calculate the variance of the Rao–Blackwellized estimator.
  2. Explain why conditioning on a sufficient statistic can reduce variance without sacrificing information about the parameter.
  3. Use the law of total variance to prove the general Rao–Blackwell variance-reduction inequality.
  4. Show that the binomial family has a complete sufficient statistic under the usual parameter space (0<p<1).
  5. Apply the Lehmann–Scheffé theorem to investigate whether (T/n) is the unique minimum-variance unbiased estimator of (p).
  6. Consider estimating (p^2). Construct an unbiased estimator and investigate how Rao–Blackwellization can improve it.
  7. Discuss the relationship between statistical sufficiency and the idea of finding compact representations of large datasets.

Hints

  • Given the total number of successes, consider how the location of those successes is distributed.
  • Information about the parameter and information about the arrangement of individual observations are not necessarily the same thing.
SET 10 / EXERCISE 02

Exercise 02 — The Prediction Errors That Are Dependent but Somehow Uncorrelated

Domain: Martingale differences · Conditional expectation · Adaptive stochastic systems

Core intuition: Conditional independence is not necessary for the errors of an adaptive stochastic process to be uncorrelated.

Scenario

A reinforcement-learning research team evaluates an adaptive agent.

At every timestep, the agent selects an action based on everything it has observed so far.

The environment produces a reward.

The research team calculates the difference between the realized reward and the reward predicted from the previous information.

The researchers assume that these differences behave like independent random variables.

You suspect that independence is too strong an assumption, but that a useful mathematical structure remains.

You propose studying martingale differences.

Technical setup

Let:

\[ \mathcal F_0\subseteq\mathcal F_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\mathcal F_T \]

be an increasing sequence of information sets, called a filtration.

Let (Y_t) represent the reward observed at timestep (t).

Define its conditional expectation:

\[ \mu_t=\mathbb E[Y_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]. \]

Define the innovation:

\[ D_t=Y_t-\mu_t. \]

Assume:

\[ \mathbb E[D_t^2]<\infty. \]

The cumulative innovation is:

\[ M_T=\sum_{t=1}^{T}D_t. \]

Research challenges

  1. Prove that:

\[ \mathbb E[D_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=0. \]

  1. Explain why this property is the defining condition of a martingale difference sequence.
  2. For (s<t), prove that:

\[ \mathbb E[D_sD_t]=0. \]

  1. Does this imply that (D_s) and (D_t) are independent? Construct a counterexample.
  2. Derive:

\[ \operatorname{Var}(M_T)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb E[D_t^2]. \]

  1. Explain why the variance decomposition remains valid despite the absence of independence.
  2. Consider a sequence where:

\[ Y_t=A_t+\epsilon_t, \]

with (A_t) chosen using previous observations and (\epsilon_t) representing new environmental randomness. Explain how conditional expectation separates predictable behavior from unpredictable innovations. 8. Why might ordinary statistical confidence intervals become unreliable if researchers incorrectly treat adaptively generated observations as independent? 9. Explain how martingale central limit theorems differ conceptually from ordinary independent-sample central limit theorems. 10. Under what additional conditions can the normalized sum of martingale differences converge approximately to a Gaussian distribution? 11. Discuss applications of martingale difference sequences in reinforcement learning, online experimentation, stochastic optimization, and sequential prediction.

Hints

  • For (s<t), the earlier innovation is already measurable with respect to the information available immediately before time (t).
  • Use the tower property of conditional expectation.
SET 10 / EXERCISE 03

Exercise 03 — Two AI Services That Fail Rarely but Fail Together

Domain: Copulas · Dependence modeling · Multivariate tail dependence

Core intuition: Knowing the marginal failure probability of two systems does not determine the probability that they fail simultaneously.

Scenario

An industrial company deploys two independent-looking AI safety systems.

System A monitors temperature anomalies.

System B monitors mechanical anomalies.

The engineers calculate that each system independently fails only 1% of the time.

They conclude that the probability of both systems failing simultaneously is approximately 0.01%.

However, both systems are exposed to the same environmental conditions.

You suspect their failures may be dependent, especially during extreme operating conditions.

You are asked to investigate how dependence changes joint reliability.

Technical setup

Let:

\[ Z_1,Z_2 \]

be standard normal random variables with correlation:

\[ \operatorname{Corr}(Z_1,Z_2)=\rho. \]

Each system fails when its latent failure score exceeds:

\[ c=\Phi^{-1}(0.99). \]

Thus:

\[ F_1={Z_1>c},\qquad F_2={Z_2>c}. \]

Each system has marginal failure probability:

\[ P(F_1)=P(F_2)=0.01. \]

The Gaussian copula is:

\[ C_\rho(u,v)=\Phi_\rho(\Phi^{-1}(u),\Phi^{-1}(v)), \]

where (\Phi_\rho) is the bivariate standard normal CDF with correlation (\rho).

Research challenges

  1. Express the simultaneous failure probability:

\[ P(F_1\cap F_2) \]

using the bivariate Gaussian CDF. 2. Calculate the joint failure probability under independence, where (\rho=0). 3. Explain how positive correlation changes the joint failure probability. 4. Derive the conditional failure probability:

\[ P(F_2\mid F_1). \]

  1. Explain why marginal failure probabilities are insufficient for evaluating redundant safety systems.
  2. Describe the role of a copula in separating marginal distributions from dependence structure.
  3. Consider the Gaussian copula with (|\rho|<1). Explain why its upper-tail dependence coefficient is zero:

\[ \lambda_U=\lim_{u\rightarrow1^-}P(V>u\mid U>u). \]

  1. Now consider a Student-t copula with (\nu) degrees of freedom and correlation parameter (\rho). Its upper-tail dependence coefficient is:

\[ \lambda_U=2t_{\nu+1}\left(-\sqrt{\frac{(\nu+1)(1-\rho)}{1+\rho}}\right). \]

Explain why the Student-t copula can exhibit asymptotic tail dependence even when its linear correlation matches that of a Gaussian copula. 9. Discuss why two dependence models with identical marginal distributions and correlation matrices can produce dramatically different simultaneous extreme-event probabilities. 10. What happens when the underlying dependence structure changes across operating regimes? 11. Design an experiment comparing Gaussian and Student-t copulas for estimating joint failures in an AI safety system. 12. Explain the consequences of incorrectly assuming independence when calculating the reliability of a system with redundant components.

Hints

  • Correlation measures a particular form of dependence, not the complete joint distribution.
  • Pay particular attention to what happens in the far upper tail rather than around the center of the distribution.
SET 10 / EXERCISE 04

Exercise 04 — The Concentration Bound That Makes a Million Experiments Unnecessary

Domain: Concentration inequalities · Hoeffding inequality · Bernstein inequality · Sub-Gaussian variables

Core intuition: The range and variance of a random variable can provide stronger finite-sample guarantees than an asymptotic normal approximation alone.

Scenario

An AI company evaluates a model using a binary success indicator.

The researchers collect thousands of observations and report the empirical success rate.

The engineering team wants a guarantee that the estimated mean is within a small distance of its true value.

A researcher proposes using a central limit theorem approximation.

You suggest examining non-asymptotic concentration inequalities, which provide finite-sample guarantees under explicit assumptions.

Technical setup

Let:

\[ X_1,\ldots,X_n \]

be independent random variables satisfying:

\[ 0\leq X_i\leq1. \]

Let:

\[ \mu=\mathbb E[X_i] \]

and:

\[ \bar X_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i. \]

Hoeffding's inequality gives:

\[ P(|\bar X_n-\mu|\geq\epsilon)\leq2e^{-2n\epsilon^2}. \]

If the variance is known to satisfy:

\[ \operatorname{Var}(X_i)\leq\sigma^2, \]

Bernstein's inequality gives:

\[ P(|\bar X_n-\mu|\geq\epsilon)\leq2\exp\left(-\frac{n\epsilon^2}{2\sigma^2+\frac23\epsilon}\right). \]

Research challenges

  1. Derive the sample-size requirement for Hoeffding's inequality to guarantee:

\[ P(|\bar X_n-\mu|\geq0.01)\leq0.05. \]

  1. Suppose the variance is known to be:

\[ \sigma^2=0.01. \]

Derive the corresponding sufficient sample-size requirement using Bernstein's inequality. 3. Compare the two bounds numerically. Why can knowledge of the variance produce a much tighter guarantee? 4. Explain the difference between a concentration inequality and a central limit theorem approximation. 5. What assumptions make Hoeffding's inequality valid? Why is boundedness important? 6. Define a sub-Gaussian random variable through its moment-generating function:

\[ \mathbb E[e^{t(X-\mathbb E[X])}]\leq e^{\sigma^2t^2/2}. \]

Explain why this condition is useful when analyzing random variables that are not necessarily bounded. 7. Compare Gaussian, sub-Gaussian, and sub-exponential tail behavior. 8. Suppose a model's errors are independent but have a heavy-tailed distribution with no finite variance. Why can the usual Bernstein inequality be inappropriate? 9. Discuss how clipping observations can produce bounded variables while changing the target expectation. 10. Explain why a statistically valid concentration guarantee may still be too conservative to be operationally useful. 11. Design an experiment comparing empirical confidence intervals based on Gaussian approximations, Hoeffding bounds, and Bernstein bounds. 12. Discuss how the distinction between asymptotic accuracy and finite-sample guarantees matters when evaluating small improvements in machine-learning systems.

Hints

  • The inequalities use different information about the distribution.
  • A theoretically valid upper bound is not necessarily close to the actual probability of error.
SET 10 / EXERCISE 05

Exercise 05 — The Pairwise Metric That Uses the Same Observation Thousands of Times

Domain: U-statistics · ROC-AUC estimation · Hoeffding decomposition

Core intuition: Constructing thousands of pairwise comparisons from a small dataset does not create thousands of independent observations.

Scenario

A research team evaluates a binary classifier using ROC-AUC.

The dataset contains a relatively small number of positive and negative examples.

The evaluation procedure compares every positive observation with every negative observation.

The team celebrates because it has generated millions of pairwise comparisons.

However, many comparisons reuse the same individual observations.

You suspect the team is overestimating the amount of independent statistical information in its evaluation.

Technical setup

Let:

\[ X_1,\ldots,X_m \]

be positive-class observations and:

\[ Y_1,\ldots,Y_n \]

be negative-class observations.

Define:

\[ h(X_i,Y_j)=\mathbf1(s(X_i)>s(Y_j))+\frac12\mathbf1(s(X_i)=s(Y_j)), \]

where (s(\cdot)) is the classifier score.

The empirical AUC is:

\[ U_{m,n}=\frac1{mn}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}h(X_i,Y_j). \]

Let:

\[ \theta=\mathbb E[h(X,Y)]. \]

Define the first-order projections:

\[ h_1(x)=\mathbb E_Y[h(x,Y)]-\theta, \]

\[ h_2(y)=\mathbb E_X[h(X,y)]-\theta. \]

Research challenges

  1. Prove that the empirical AUC is an unbiased estimator of the population AUC:

\[ \mathbb E[U_{m,n}]=\theta. \]

  1. Consider two positive scores:

\[ X_1=0.8,\qquad X_2=0.6, \]

and two negative scores:

\[ Y_1=0.7,\qquad Y_2=0.4. \]

Calculate the empirical AUC. 3. Explain why the (mn) pairwise comparisons are not mutually independent. 4. Derive the first-order Hoeffding decomposition of the two-sample U-statistic. 5. Show that, under suitable non-degeneracy conditions:

\[ \operatorname{Var}(U_{m,n})\approx\frac{\operatorname{Var}(h_1(X))}{m}+\frac{\operatorname{Var}(h_2(Y))}{n}. \]

  1. Explain why the precision of the estimator depends separately on the number of positive and negative examples.
  2. What happens when one class is extremely rare, even if the total number of pairwise comparisons is large?
  3. Define a degenerate U-statistic and explain why the first-order approximation can fail in that case.
  4. Discuss why treating every pairwise comparison as an independent Bernoulli observation gives an incorrect standard error.
  5. Compare the U-statistic interpretation of AUC with ordinary sample-mean estimation.
  6. Design an evaluation procedure that estimates AUC uncertainty while respecting the dependence induced by shared observations.

Hints

  • Every positive observation participates in (n) comparisons.
  • Decompose each pairwise kernel into its overall expectation, its positive-observation contribution, its negative-observation contribution, and a residual interaction term.
SET 10 / EXERCISE 06

Exercise 06 — The Average That Collapses When One Extreme Observation Appears

Domain: Robust statistics · Influence functions · Breakdown points · M-estimation

Core intuition: An estimator can be highly efficient under an ideal statistical model but catastrophically unstable under small amounts of contamination.

Scenario

A research laboratory analyzes the distribution of prediction errors produced by an AI system.

Most observations are small.

However, a few corrupted measurements contain extremely large values.

The ordinary mean changes dramatically after adding only one corrupted observation.

The team does not want to discard all large errors because some could represent genuine model failures.

You are asked to compare the robustness of different estimators.

Technical setup

Assume the uncontaminated population follows:

\[ X\sim\mathcal N(0,1). \]

Consider the contaminated distribution:

\[ P_\varepsilon=(1-\varepsilon)P+\varepsilon\delta_M, \]

where:

  • (\varepsilon) is the contamination fraction.
  • (\delta_M) is a point mass at an extreme value (M).

For an estimator (T(P)), define its influence function:

\[ \operatorname{IF}(z;T,P)=\lim_{\varepsilon\rightarrow0}\frac{T((1-\varepsilon)P+\varepsilon\delta_z)-T(P)}{\varepsilon}. \]

Research challenges

  1. Derive the population mean under the contaminated distribution.
  2. Calculate the influence function of the sample mean functional.
  3. Explain why the mean has an unbounded influence function.
  4. Determine the population median under sufficiently small contamination at an extreme positive value.
  5. Derive the influence function of the median:

\[ \operatorname{IF}(z;\operatorname{Med},P)=\frac{\frac12-\mathbf1(z\leq m)}{f(m)}, \]

assuming a positive continuous density at the median (m). 6. Calculate its maximum absolute influence under the standard normal distribution. 7. Explain the breakdown point and compare the mean and median. 8. Consider the Huber score function:

\[ \psi_c(u)=\begin{cases}-c&u<-c,\u&|u|\leq c,\c&u>c.\end{cases} \]

Explain how an M-estimator based on this function limits the contribution of extreme observations. 9. For a known scale of one and the uncontaminated standard normal model, derive the influence function of the corresponding Huber location estimator. 10. Explain the trade-off between robustness and statistical efficiency under uncontaminated Gaussian data. 11. Why does automatically removing every extreme observation risk deleting genuine rare failures? 12. Design an experiment comparing the mean, median, and Huber estimator under several contamination fractions and contamination magnitudes.

Hints

  • Differentiate the estimator as a functional of the underlying probability distribution.
  • Robustness is about sensitivity to contamination, not simply the magnitude of the observed values.
SET 10 / EXERCISE 07

Exercise 07 — The Model That Wins Against Every Other Model but Still Has Weak Statistical Evidence

Domain: Bayesian model evidence · Bayes factors · Laplace approximation · Occam's factor

Core intuition: Bayesian model comparison rewards good fit while penalizing models that spread prior probability over large regions of parameter space that the data do not support.

Scenario

A research group compares two probabilistic models.

Model A is a simple model with no adjustable parameter.

Model B introduces an additional parameter that can explain small deviations in the observations.

Model B achieves a better maximum likelihood.

The team immediately declares it superior.

You argue that evaluating only the best possible parameter value ignores how much prior parameter space the model allocated to explanations that fit the observations poorly.

You propose comparing marginal likelihoods instead.

Technical setup

Suppose:

\[ Y_i\mid\theta\sim\mathcal N(\theta,1). \]

Compare:

Model (M_0):

\[ \theta=0. \]

Model (M_1):

\[ \theta\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau^2),\qquad\tau^2=4. \]

The dataset contains:

\[ n=25 \]

observations with:

\[ \bar Y=0.4. \]

The Bayes factor is:

\[ BF_{10}=\frac{p(Y\mid M_1)}{p(Y\mid M_0)}. \]

Research challenges

  1. Calculate the maximum-likelihood estimate of (\theta) under (M_1).
  2. Compare the maximized likelihoods of (M_0) and (M_1).
  3. Derive the marginal likelihood:

\[ p(Y\mid M_1)=\int p(Y\mid\theta,M_1)p(\theta\mid M_1),d\theta. \]

  1. Use Gaussian conjugacy to derive the distribution of the sample mean under the two models.
  2. Show that the residual component of the likelihood cancels in the Bayes factor.
  3. Derive:

\[ BF_{10}=\sqrt{\frac{1/n}{\tau^2+1/n}}\exp\left[\frac{\bar Y^2}{2}\left(n-\frac{1}{\tau^2+1/n}\right)\right]. \]

  1. Evaluate the expression numerically for the supplied data.
  2. Explain why a model can have a larger maximum likelihood while receiving a smaller Bayes factor.
  3. Interpret the determinant or volume term appearing in the marginal likelihood as an Occam factor.
  4. Explain how changing the prior variance (\tau^2) can alter the Bayes factor even when the observed data remain unchanged.
  5. Compare marginal-likelihood model selection with AIC and BIC. What different approximations or philosophical objectives do these criteria use?
  6. Derive the general Laplace approximation:

\[ p(Y\mid M)\approx p(Y\mid\hat\theta,M)p(\hat\theta\mid M)(2\pi)^{d/2}|H(\hat\theta)|^{-1/2}, \]

where (H) is the Hessian of the negative log posterior or the corresponding local negative log integrand. 13. Discuss why Laplace approximation can fail when the likelihood has multiple modes, strong asymmetry, or singular structure.

Hints

  • Maximum likelihood asks for the best-fitting parameter value.
  • Marginal likelihood averages the likelihood over the entire prior distribution.
SET 10 / EXERCISE 08

Exercise 08 — One Infrastructure Failure That Creates Five More

Domain: Branching processes · Galton–Watson processes · Cascade probability

Core intuition: A failure process can become self-sustaining when each failure generates, on average, more than one additional failure.

Scenario

A large AI company operates a distributed computing cluster.

A server failure can overload neighboring servers.

An overloaded server may then fail, creating additional load on other machines.

The engineering team estimates the average number of secondary failures generated by one failed server.

They ask whether the cluster will eventually recover or whether an initial failure can trigger an unlimited cascade.

You propose modeling the process as a branching process.

Technical setup

Consider a Galton–Watson branching process.

Initially:

\[ Z_0=1. \]

Each failed unit independently produces a random number of additional failures.

Assume the number of offspring follows:

\[ N\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(m). \]

Thus:

\[ P(N=k)=e^{-m}\frac{m^k}{k!}. \]

Let (Z_t) denote the number of failures in generation (t).

The probability-generating function is:

\[ G(s)=\mathbb E[s^N]. \]

The extinction probability (q) satisfies:

\[ q=G(q). \]

Research challenges

  1. Derive the probability-generating function for the Poisson offspring distribution.
  2. Establish the recursive relationship between the generation sizes.
  3. Derive the equation:

\[ q=e^{m(q-1)}. \]

  1. Explain why (q=1) is always a solution.

  2. Show that:

    • If (m\leq1), extinction occurs with probability one under the usual non-degeneracy conditions.
    • If (m>1), extinction has probability less than one.

  3. For (m=0.8), derive the expected total number of failures across all generations.

  4. Calculate that expected total.

  5. Explain why an expected finite cascade size does not imply that every cascade is small.

  6. For (m=1.2), explain why the extinction probability satisfies a nontrivial fixed-point equation.

  7. Estimate the smaller solution of:

\[ q=e^{1.2(q-1)}. \]

  1. Suppose an engineering intervention reduces the average number of secondary failures per failed server from 1.2 to 0.9. Analyze how fundamentally this changes system reliability.
  2. Discuss the limitations of the independent-offspring assumption when failures occur in a network with heterogeneous connectivity and shared environmental conditions.
  3. Design an experiment to estimate the effective reproduction number of cascading failures in a distributed AI system.

Hints

  • Extinction probability is determined by a fixed point of the offspring generating function.
  • The expected total cascade size and the probability of eventual extinction are related but distinct quantities.
SET 10 / EXERCISE 09

Exercise 09 — Detecting a Distribution Shift Without Knowing What the Correct Distribution Should Look Like

Domain: Maximum Mean Discrepancy · Kernel two-sample testing · Permutation inference

Core intuition: Two distributions can be compared through their mean embeddings in a reproducing-kernel Hilbert space, allowing statistical testing without explicitly estimating their probability densities.

Scenario

An AI company deploys a model in two environments.

Environment A represents the original training distribution.

Environment B represents live production traffic.

The model performs well initially, but the engineers suspect that the input distribution has changed.

They do not know the correct parametric distribution for either environment.

They need a statistical test that determines whether the two sample populations differ.

You propose maximum mean discrepancy.

Technical setup

Let:

\[ X_1,\ldots,X_m\sim P \]

and:

\[ Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\sim Q. \]

Let (k) be a positive-definite kernel with feature map:

\[ \phi(x) \]

into a reproducing-kernel Hilbert space.

Define the kernel mean embeddings:

\[ \mu_P=\mathbb E_P[\phi(X)], \]

\[ \mu_Q=\mathbb E_Q[\phi(Y)]. \]

Maximum mean discrepancy is:

\[ \operatorname{MMD}(P,Q)=|\mu_P-\mu_Q|_{\mathcal H}. \]

Its squared population form is:

\[ \operatorname{MMD}^2(P,Q)=\mathbb E[k(X,X')]+\mathbb E[k(Y,Y')]-2\mathbb E[k(X,Y)]. \]

Research challenges

  1. Derive the population MMD expression from the squared Hilbert-space norm.
  2. Explain why MMD compares distributions through their expected feature representations.
  3. Derive the unbiased empirical estimator:

\[ \widehat{\operatorname{MMD}}_u^2=\frac{1}{m(m-1)}\sum_{i\neq j}k(X_i,X_j)+\frac{1}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i\neq j}k(Y_i,Y_j)-\frac{2}{mn}\sum_{i,j}k(X_i,Y_j). \]

  1. Explain why this unbiased estimator can be negative in finite samples even though the population MMD squared cannot be negative.
  2. Distinguish characteristic kernels from kernels that fail to uniquely identify distributions through their mean embeddings.
  3. Why is a Gaussian RBF kernel characteristic under the standard Euclidean-domain assumptions?
  4. Explain how the kernel bandwidth influences the scale of differences the test is sensitive to.
  5. Suppose the two environments have identical means but different variances. Explain why a linear kernel may fail to detect their difference while a suitable nonlinear kernel can succeed.
  6. Derive the permutation-testing procedure under the null hypothesis:

\[ H_0:P=Q. \]

Why is exchangeability important? 10. Explain why a permutation test can provide a valid nonparametric significance assessment without specifying the distribution of the observations. 11. What problems arise when the kernel bandwidth is selected using the same observed samples and is not accounted for in the test calibration? 12. Design an MMD-based monitoring strategy for detecting distribution changes in production AI systems while controlling false alarms across repeated monitoring windows.

Hints

  • The mean embedding is an expectation of feature vectors, not an expectation of the raw observations alone.
  • Under the null hypothesis, the labels indicating which sample came from which distribution are exchangeable.
SET 10 / EXERCISE 10

Exercise 10 — Finding an Unknown Root Using Only Noisy Observations

Domain: Stochastic approximation · Robbins–Monro algorithm · Convergence conditions

Core intuition: A stochastic algorithm can approach an unknown solution without ever observing the exact function it is trying to solve.

Scenario

A machine-learning laboratory develops an adaptive sensor-calibration system.

The ideal calibration parameter is defined as the root of a function representing the expected sensor response.

However, each evaluation of the function is noisy because the sensor is affected by random environmental conditions.

The engineering team cannot calculate the exact expected function.

They only receive noisy measurements.

You are asked to design an iterative procedure that finds the required parameter using these observations.

Technical setup

Consider finding a solution to:

\[ g(\theta)=0. \]

Suppose the available observation is:

\[ H(\theta,\xi), \]

where:

\[ \mathbb E[H(\theta,\xi)]=g(\theta). \]

Consider the update:

\[ \theta_{t+1}=\theta_t-a_tH(\theta_t,\xi_{t+1}). \]

For the concrete example, suppose:

\[ g(\theta)=\theta^2-2, \]

and:

\[ H(\theta,\xi)=\theta^2-2+\xi, \]

where:

\[ \mathbb E[\xi]=0,\qquad\operatorname{Var}(\xi)=\sigma^2<\infty. \]

The positive root is:

\[ \theta^*=\sqrt2. \]

Consider step sizes:

\[ a_t=\frac{a}{t+1}. \]

Research challenges

  1. Verify that the noisy observation is an unbiased estimate of the root function.
  2. Write the explicit stochastic update.
  3. Explain why the algorithm moves toward a root when its expected drift points in the appropriate direction.
  4. Linearize the expected update around the positive root and investigate local stability.
  5. Calculate:

\[ g'(\theta^*). \]

What does its sign imply? 6. Compare a constant step size:

\[ a_t=a \]

with a decreasing step size.

Why can constant-step stochastic approximation continue fluctuating around the root even after many iterations? 7. Explain the significance of the Robbins–Monro conditions:

\[ \sum_{t=0}^{\infty}a_t=\infty, \]

\[ \sum_{t=0}^{\infty}a_t^2<\infty. \]

  1. Verify whether the proposed harmonic step-size schedule satisfies both conditions.
  2. Explain why a step-size sequence that decreases too quickly may prevent the algorithm from fully correcting an initial estimation error.
  3. Discuss the assumptions on the noise process that are needed to establish convergence.
  4. The function (g(\theta)=\theta^2-2) has two roots. Explain why the initialization and stability of the expected dynamics matter when determining which root is reached.
  5. Suppose the sensor noise variance changes over time. How might this affect the appropriate step-size schedule?
  6. Design an experiment comparing stochastic approximation with ordinary root finding when noisy function evaluations are the only available information.

Hints

  • Separate the expected drift from the random innovation.
  • The direction of local stability is determined by the derivative of the expected root function around the solution.

End of Problem Set 10

Probability & Statistics research territory map

# Research territory Main intellectual skill
01 Sufficient statistics and Rao–Blackwellization Extracting information while reducing estimator variance
02 Martingale differences Reasoning about adaptively generated stochastic observations
03 Copulas Understanding nonlinear dependence and joint tail risk
04 Concentration inequalities Obtaining finite-sample guarantees
05 U-statistics Handling pairwise estimators with dependent comparisons
06 Robust statistics Measuring sensitivity to contamination
07 Bayesian model evidence Understanding marginal likelihood and Occam's factor
08 Branching processes Analyzing cascading stochastic failures
09 Maximum Mean Discrepancy Performing nonparametric distribution comparison
10 Stochastic approximation Finding unknown solutions using noisy observations

Final research standard

Every solution should contain four distinct layers.

1. Probability foundations

Can you reason correctly about conditional expectation, dependence, distributions, and stochastic behavior?

2. Statistical structure

Can you identify sufficient information, estimator properties, dependence mechanisms, and statistical limitations?

3. Mathematical investigation

Can you derive the relevant identities, establish convergence or error guarantees, and construct counterexamples?

4. Research application

Can you use the mathematical result to improve an AI experiment, diagnose a model, design an algorithm, or challenge an existing methodology?

The final challenge

A researcher should be able to look at a sophisticated AI system and question:

  • Is there a more informative statistic hidden in the data?
  • Are our observations independent, or merely uncorrelated?
  • Are two systems genuinely independent in their extreme failures?
  • Does our estimator exploit all available information?
  • Can a few corrupted observations dominate our conclusions?
  • Does our evidence support the model itself or only a particular parameter configuration?
  • Can we discover distributional differences without assuming a parametric family?
  • Can an algorithm converge when the underlying function is available only through noisy measurements?

The goal is not to become someone who knows hundreds of statistical methods. It is to become someone who understands the mathematical conditions under which those methods deserve to be trusted.

Transformer EngineeringCOLLECTION 11 / 15

Problem Set 11 — Transformer Architecture Design: From Mathematical Mechanisms to Research-Level Engineering Decisions

Transformer architecture design and research-level engineering decisions

Difficulty: Advanced Graduate → PhD

Objective: Develop the ability to design, analyze, modify, and defend Transformer architectures under mathematical, computational, and practical constraints.

General instructions

You are an architectural researcher, not simply an architecture user. Every exercise presents an engineering or research scenario in which you must make decisions about the internal structure of a Transformer. For every proposed design, explain:

Why the architecture is appropriate for the problem. What mathematical properties it introduces. What computational resources it consumes. What expressive capabilities it preserves or sacrifices. What failure modes could emerge. How you would experimentally validate your design.

No coding is required. No solutions are provided.

SET 11 / EXERCISE 01

Exercise 01 — Designing a Transformer That Can Survive 500 Layers

Domain: Transformer depth · Residual topology · Pre-LN versus Post-LN · Gradient propagation

Core intuition: The placement of normalization relative to residual connections changes the mathematical structure of information and gradient propagation through a deep Transformer.

Scenario

A research laboratory wants to build a 500-layer Transformer for scientific reasoning. The current architecture uses conventional residual blocks with normalization after the residual addition. Training becomes increasingly unstable as depth increases. The team attempts to solve the problem by reducing the learning rate, but performance remains disappointing. You suspect that the issue is partly architectural. You are asked to compare alternative residual and normalization arrangements before proposing a deeper architecture.

Technical setup

Consider a Transformer sublayer represented abstractly by:

\[F\ell(x\ell).\]

Two candidate architectures are:

Architecture A — Post-LayerNorm:

\operatorname{LN} \left( x\ell+F\ell(x_\ell) \right). ] Architecture B — Pre-LayerNorm: x\ell+F\ell(\operatorname{LN}(x_\ell)). ] For a simplified local linearization, let:

\[J_\ell\]

denote the Jacobian of the sublayer, and let:

\[N_\ell\]

denote the Jacobian of LayerNorm at the relevant activation. For simplicity, initially treat the input as a vector in (\mathbb R^d).

Research challenges

  • Derive the Jacobian of one Pre-LN residual block.
  • Derive the Jacobian of one Post-LN residual block.
  • Express the gradient propagation through (L) consecutive Pre-LN blocks as a product of Jacobian factors.
  • Explain why the identity residual path can provide a direct gradient route through a Pre-LN network.
  • Does the existence of an identity path guarantee perfectly stable gradients? Explain which additional factors still affect the result.
  • Investigate the consequences of repeatedly applying normalization after residual addition in a very deep architecture.
  • Suppose the residual branch is scaled: x\ell+\alpha\ell F\ell(x\ell).
  • Explain how the choice of (\alpha_\ell) can affect the accumulated transformation across hundreds of layers.
  • Compare constant residual scaling with depth-dependent residual scaling.
  • The research team wants to preserve the magnitude and information carried by the residual stream. What would you measure to determine whether a proposed normalization strategy is excessively modifying the stream?
  • Explain why increasing the number of layers does not automatically increase the useful computational depth of a Transformer.
  • Propose an experimental design comparing Pre-LN, Post-LN, and scaled residual architectures while controlling model size and training compute.

Hints

Analyze the identity component of the Jacobian separately from the transformation introduced by the sublayer.

Stability across one block does not automatically imply stability across hundreds of compositions.

SET 11 / EXERCISE 02

Exercise 02 — Should Your Transformer Have 8 Heads, 32 Heads, or 128 Heads?

Domain: Multi-head attention · Attention-head dimensionality · Architectural capacity

Core intuition: The number of attention heads controls the number of independently parameterized attention patterns, while the head dimension controls the feature capacity available to each individual head.

Scenario

A research team develops a Transformer for complex scientific documents. The model has a hidden dimension of:

\[d_{\mathrm{model}}=1024.\]

The architecture currently uses 16 attention heads. A researcher proposes increasing the number of heads to 64 because they believe more heads automatically mean more sophisticated reasoning. Another researcher proposes decreasing the number to 8, arguing that each head would have more representational capacity. You are asked to analyze the actual trade-offs.

Technical setup

For standard multi-head self-attention:

\[Q=XW_Q,\qquad K=XW_K,\qquad V=XW_V.\]

Assume:

\[d_k=d_v=d_h\]

and:

\[h dh=d{\mathrm{model}}.\]

Each head computes:

\operatorname{softmax} \left( \frac{Q_iK_i^\top}{\sqrt{d_h}} \right)V_i. ] The head outputs are concatenated and projected: \operatorname{Concat} (\operatorname{head}_1,\ldots,\operatorname{head}_h)W_O. ] Consider three candidate configurations:

Configuration Heads (h) Head dimension (d_h)

A 8 128

B 16 64

C 64 16

Research challenges

  • Verify that all three configurations have the same total attention dimension.
  • Derive the parameter count of the four standard attention projection matrices, assuming biases are omitted.
  • Explain why the total projection parameter count can remain constant even when the number of heads changes.
  • Compare the attention-score computation cost across the three configurations for sequence length (T).
  • Explain what changes when each head receives only 16 dimensions instead of 128.
  • Suppose two heads learn exactly the same attention distribution and their output projections contain redundant components. Explain why increasing the number of heads does not necessarily increase useful representational capacity.
  • Construct a simplified example where two heads attend to different token relationships and therefore provide complementary information.
  • What role does the scaling factor: \[\frac1{\sqrt{d_h}}\] play when the head dimension changes?
  • A researcher proposes assigning different dimensions to different heads rather than using equal head dimensions. What architectural advantages and implementation difficulties could this introduce?
  • Design an ablation study that isolates the effect of head count from the effect of total model width.
  • Propose metrics for investigating head redundancy, attention-pattern diversity, and downstream contribution.
  • Under what circumstances might fewer, wider heads be preferable to many narrow heads?

Hints

Keep total attention width fixed when comparing head counts.

More independent attention distributions do not automatically imply more independent information.

SET 11 / EXERCISE 03

Exercise 03 — The Transformer That Runs Out of Memory Before It Finishes Generating

Domain: Grouped-Query Attention · Multi-Query Attention · KV-cache architecture

Core intuition: During autoregressive inference, sharing key-value projections can dramatically reduce memory consumption without changing the autoregressive dependency structure.

Scenario

A company deploys a 32-layer language model with:

\[d_{\mathrm{model}}=4096.\]

Its inference system supports eight simultaneous users, each maintaining an 8,192-token context. The model becomes memory-bound during generation because it must retain key and value representations for previously processed tokens. The engineering team proposes reducing the number of KV heads while retaining the number of query heads. You are asked to design an appropriate attention configuration.

Technical setup

The architecture has:

(n_q=32) query heads.

(d_h=128).

(L=32) layers.

Batch size (B=8).

Context length (T=8192).

FP16 KV-cache elements, requiring 2 bytes each.

Consider three architectures:

Multi-Head Attention (MHA):

\[n_{kv}=32.\]

Grouped-Query Attention (GQA):

\[n_{kv}=8.\]

Multi-Query Attention (MQA):

\[n_{kv}=1.\]

The number of elements stored in the complete KV cache is:

2BLTn_{kv}d_h. ] The factor 2 accounts for keys and values.

Research challenges

  • Calculate the total KV-cache memory required by MHA.
  • Calculate the corresponding memory requirements for GQA and MQA.
  • Express the memory reduction factor of GQA and MQA relative to MHA.
  • Explain why the query-head count can remain 32 even when only eight KV heads are stored.
  • Describe how query heads are assigned to groups of shared KV heads.
  • Analyze the distinction between sharing keys only, sharing values only, and sharing both keys and values.
  • Why does reducing KV heads primarily improve inference memory requirements rather than eliminating the main query-key interaction?
  • Suppose the number of simultaneous users doubles while context length remains constant. Derive the effect on KV-cache memory.
  • Suppose context length doubles while batch size remains constant. Explain why the cache becomes a major scalability bottleneck.
  • Investigate what representational flexibility could be lost when several query heads use the same key-value representation.
  • Design an experiment comparing MHA, GQA, and MQA using identical query-head count, model width, and training data.
  • Propose a criterion for choosing the number of KV heads when latency, memory, and generation quality must be optimized simultaneously.

Hints

Distinguish the number of independently generated queries from the number of stored key-value representations.

Cache memory grows linearly with context length, batch size, layer count, and KV-head count.

SET 11 / EXERCISE 04

Exercise 04 — Calculating Attention Without Ever Constructing the Attention Matrix

Domain: FlashAttention · Online softmax · IO-aware algorithms

Core intuition: An algorithm can calculate the exact mathematical result of attention while avoiding the materialization of its enormous intermediate attention matrix.

Scenario

A research laboratory trains a Transformer on sequences of 32,768 tokens. The ordinary attention implementation computes:

\[A=\operatorname{softmax}\ \left(\ \frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\ \right).\]

The matrix (A) contains billions of attention scores for sufficiently large batches. The team discovers that storing and repeatedly transferring this matrix is a major computational bottleneck. A researcher proposes dividing queries, keys, and values into blocks and maintaining an online softmax calculation. You are asked to derive how this can work without changing the exact attention result.

Technical setup

For a query vector (q), define the attention scores:

\[s_j=\frac{q^\top k_j}{\sqrt{d_k}}.\]

The desired output is:

\[o=\ \frac{\ \sum{j=1}^{T}e^{s_j}v_j\ }{\ \sum{j=1}^{T}e^{s_j}\ }.\]

Process the keys and values in blocks. After processing a set of blocks, maintain:

Running maximum (m).

Running normalizer (\ell).

Running weighted output vector (u).

Initially:

\[m=-\infty,\qquad\ \ell=0,\qquad\ u=0.\]

For a newly processed block of scores (s_j), define:

\[m'=\max(m,\max_j s_j).\]

The online updates are:

e^{m-m'}\ell

\sum_j e^{s_j-m'}, ]

e^{m-m'}u

\sum_j e^{s_j-m'}v_j. ]

The final attention output is:

\[o=\frac{u}{\ell}.\]

Research challenges

  • Derive the online normalizer update from the ordinary softmax denominator.
  • Derive the online weighted-output update.
  • Prove that after processing every block, the ratio: \[\frac{u}{\ell}\] is exactly equal to the ordinary softmax attention output, up to floating-point effects.
  • Explain why maintaining a running maximum improves numerical stability.
  • What would go wrong if the online algorithm simply summed exponentials without adjusting previously accumulated values when a larger maximum appears?
  • For a sequence of length (T), calculate the number of attention scores that would be materialized in a conventional implementation.
  • Explain the difference between arithmetic complexity and memory-I/O complexity.
  • Describe why tiled computation can reduce transfers between high-bandwidth memory and faster on-chip memory.
  • Compare the asymptotic memory requirements of materialized attention and tiled exact attention.
  • Suppose the query block size and key block size are increased. Explain the trade-off between on-chip memory requirements and data reuse.
  • Why does a memory-efficient exact attention algorithm still have quadratic attention arithmetic in the sequence length?
  • Propose an experiment comparing conventional attention and tiled attention using peak memory, data movement, throughput, and numerical agreement.

Hints

Maintain a shared exponential reference point for every block.

When the reference maximum changes, rescale everything accumulated using the previous maximum.

SET 11 / EXERCISE 05

Exercise 05 — Building a Transformer That Can Read a Million Tokens

Domain: Sparse attention · Local-global communication · Long-context architecture design

Core intuition: Reducing attention connectivity can lower computational cost dramatically, but the pattern of allowed interactions determines how quickly information can travel through the architecture.

Scenario

A research company wants to develop a Transformer that processes extremely long scientific documents. Full self-attention is too expensive:

\[O(T^2d).\]

The team proposes local attention, where each token can interact only with nearby tokens. However, they realize that a definition introduced at the beginning of a million-token document might need to influence a conclusion near the end. A purely local architecture may struggle to move information over such distances. You are asked to design a sparse attention architecture that combines local communication with global information exchange.

Technical setup

Let the sequence length be:

\[T=1,000,000.\]

Each ordinary token can attend to:

(r=128) tokens on either side.

(g=16) global tokens.

Each global token can attend to every ordinary token. Assume attention edges are directed from query positions to the key positions they can access. Ignoring boundary effects, the total attention-score count per layer is approximately:

\[N_{\mathrm{scores}}\ \approx\ T(2r+1+g)+gT.\]

Research challenges

  • Derive the approximate number of attention scores per layer.
  • Compare its computational scaling with full self-attention.
  • Calculate the number of scores using the specified values.
  • Explain how local attention preserves short-range information while reducing the number of interactions.
  • Suppose a token near the beginning needs to communicate information to a token near the end. How many ordinary local-attention layers would be required in the worst case if each layer can propagate information across a maximum distance of (r)?
  • Explain how global tokens can reduce this communication path length.
  • Consider the following two-layer process:
  • Global tokens aggregate information from all ordinary tokens.
  • Ordinary tokens receive information from global tokens.
  • Explain why information can travel between distant ordinary tokens through this mechanism.
  • Why can a small number of global tokens become an information bottleneck even when they attend to the entire sequence?
  • Propose a hierarchical architecture in which local regions first produce summary representations, which are then processed by global layers.
  • Compare fixed local windows, dilated windows, and hierarchical attention in terms of connectivity and computational complexity.
  • Explain why sparse attention patterns should be evaluated for information accessibility, not merely for FLOP reduction.
  • Design an experiment measuring long-range information retrieval as a function of sequence distance, global-token count, and local window size.

Hints

Attention connectivity can be interpreted as a communication graph between token representations.

A short communication path does not guarantee that the transmitted information has been preserved faithfully.

SET 11 / EXERCISE 06

Exercise 06 — Combining Images, Audio, and Text Without Letting One Modality Dominate

Domain: Cross-attention · Multimodal fusion · Latent bottleneck architecture

Core intuition: The direction of cross-attention and the number of shared latent representations determine how modalities exchange information and how much computation is required.

Scenario

A research laboratory develops a scientific assistant that processes:

An image containing experimental measurements.

A long audio recording explaining the experiment.

A textual description of the research question.

The raw sequence lengths are:

Modality Number of tokens

Image 4096

Audio 8192

Text 1024

The research team initially concatenates all tokens and applies full self-attention. The computational cost becomes excessive. A researcher proposes a shared latent bottleneck that receives information from each modality through cross-attention. You are asked to design and analyze the alternative architecture.

Technical setup

Let:

\[X_I\in\mathbb R^{4096\times d},\]

\[X_A\in\mathbb R^{8192\times d},\]

\[X_T\in\mathbb R^{1024\times d}.\]

Introduce:

\[M\in\mathbb R^{N_m\times d}\]

learnable latent queries. For a source modality (X), the latent update is: M+ \operatorname{Attention} (MW_Q,XW_K,XW_V). ] Assume that all projections have compatible dimensions and that the latent queries attend to every token of the selected modality. For cross-attention between (N_q) queries and (N_k) source tokens, the attention-score computation scales as:

\[O(N_qN_kd).\]

Research challenges

  • Calculate the full self-attention interaction count when all three modalities are concatenated.
  • Calculate the total interaction count when the shared latent bottleneck has: \[N_m=256\] and independently cross-attends to the three modalities.
  • Compare the two approaches mathematically.
  • Explain why latent-query cross-attention avoids constructing a fully connected attention matrix over all raw tokens.
  • Compare early fusion through token concatenation with late fusion through separate modality encoders.
  • Suppose the image modality contains important spatial relationships. What could be lost if it is compressed too aggressively before fusion?
  • Should the three modalities be processed using identical encoders? Defend your decision based on their different input structures.
  • Compare unidirectional cross-attention with bidirectional cross-attention. What additional computational and representational flexibility does bidirectional exchange provide?
  • Explain how missing modalities could be handled when the latent representation receives information from multiple independent sources.
  • Suppose audio tokens substantially outnumber image tokens. Why does token count alone not determine how much influence each modality should have?
  • Design a modality-balancing strategy that prevents one source from dominating the shared latent representation.
  • Propose an evaluation protocol measuring modality-specific performance, cross-modal reasoning, missing-modality robustness, and computational cost.

Hints

Distinguish the number of source tokens from the number of query representations.

The bottleneck reduces interaction complexity, but it also restricts how much information can be retained.

SET 11 / EXERCISE 07

Exercise 07 — Should the Transformer Normalize the Mean Away?

Domain: LayerNorm · RMSNorm · Activation statistics · Normalization geometry

Core intuition: Normalization is not a neutral operation; its invariances determine which information is preserved and which information is removed from the residual representation.

Scenario

A research team develops a Transformer for scientific sequence modeling. The hidden representations contain large-scale magnitude variations, and the team wants to improve optimization stability. One researcher proposes LayerNorm. Another proposes RMSNorm, arguing that subtracting the feature mean is unnecessary. You are asked to determine what information each normalization operation removes or preserves.

Technical setup

For:

\[x\in\mathbb R^d,\]

define its mean:

\[\mu(x)=\frac1d\sum_{i=1}^{d}x_i.\]

LayerNorm is:

\frac{x-\mu(x)\mathbf1} {\sqrt{ \frac1d|x-\mu(x)\mathbf1|_2^2+\epsilon }} \odot\gamma+\beta. ] RMSNorm is: \frac{x} {\sqrt{ \frac1d|x|_2^2+\epsilon }} \odot\gamma. ] Initially, ignore the affine parameters (\gamma,\beta) and take:

\[\epsilon\rightarrow0.\]

Research challenges

  • Derive the output of LayerNorm for a general vector (x).
  • Derive the output of RMSNorm.
  • Calculate both normalizations for: \[x= \ \begin{pmatrix} \ 2\ \ 4\ \ 6 \ \end{pmatrix}.\]
  • Prove that LayerNorm removes any constant shift:
  • \operatorname{LN}(x).
  • Explain why RMSNorm does not possess the same shift invariance.
  • Show that both normalizations are invariant to multiplication by a positive scalar under the stated simplifications.
  • What information about the original activation is lost after LayerNorm that may remain partially encoded after RMSNorm?
  • Explain why preserving mean-related information could matter in a residual-stream architecture.
  • Compare the computational requirements of LayerNorm and RMSNorm.
  • Why does the presence of learnable affine parameters alter some of the simple invariance arguments?
  • Design an experiment in which activation mean contains task-relevant information. Compare the consequences of applying LayerNorm and RMSNorm.
  • Under what circumstances might LayerNorm be preferable despite its removal of the feature mean?

Hints

Examine the transformation of a vector under adding a constant in every coordinate.

Normalization should be analyzed as a geometric transformation, not simply a numerical stabilization trick.

SET 11 / EXERCISE 08

Exercise 08 — Should the Input Embeddings and Output Classifier Share the Same Weights?

Domain: Token embeddings · Weight tying · Vocabulary projection · Parameter sharing

Core intuition: Sharing the input embedding matrix with the output projection imposes a relationship between how tokens are represented and how tokens are predicted.

Scenario

A company develops a language model with a vocabulary containing 200,000 tokens. The model has:

\[d_{\mathrm{model}}=2048.\]

The architecture uses an embedding matrix to convert token IDs into continuous vectors and an output projection to calculate vocabulary logits. The research team notices that these two matrices contain an enormous number of parameters. One researcher proposes sharing them. Another argues that the model should learn input representations and output classification weights independently. You are asked to analyze the architectural implications.

Technical setup

Let:

\[E\in\mathbb R^{V\times d}\]

be the input embedding matrix. For token ID (i):

\[xi=E{i,:}.\]

Let the final hidden state be:

\[h\in\mathbb R^d.\]

With an independent output matrix:

\[W_{\mathrm{out}}\in\mathbb R^{V\times d},\]

the logits are:

\[z=W_{\mathrm{out}}h+b.\]

Weight tying imposes:

\[W_{\mathrm{out}}=E.\]

Research challenges

  • Calculate the number of parameters in the independent input and output matrices.
  • Calculate the number of parameters saved through weight tying.
  • Express the output logits under weight tying: \[z=Eh+b.\]
  • Explain why the logit for a token is directly related to the similarity between the final hidden state and its embedding vector.
  • Derive the gradient contributions to a shared embedding matrix from both:
  • Input-token usage.
  • Output-token prediction.
  • Explain why combining these gradient contributions can be beneficial.
  • Construct a scenario in which the optimal geometry of input embeddings conflicts with the optimal geometry of output classifiers.
  • How could such a conflict affect rare tokens that appear infrequently as inputs but need accurate output predictions?
  • Explain why weight tying changes the hypothesis class of the model rather than merely reducing storage.
  • Compare shared and independent embeddings under a highly imbalanced vocabulary distribution.
  • Propose an intermediate design in which some embedding parameters are shared while others are independently trainable.
  • Design an experiment comparing perplexity, parameter count, rare-token prediction, and representation geometry under tied and untied configurations.

Hints

The same parameter matrix receives learning signals from two different roles.

Parameter sharing introduces a mathematical constraint on the relationship between those roles.

SET 11 / EXERCISE 09

Exercise 09 — Predicting a Million Different Tokens Without Computing a Million Logits Every Time

Domain: Adaptive softmax · Hierarchical output layers · Vocabulary-dependent computation

Core intuition: The output distribution of a language model can be structured so that frequent tokens are cheap to predict while rare tokens are handled through more specialized computations.

Scenario

A research laboratory develops a multilingual model with a vocabulary of one million tokens. A standard output projection requires computing:

\[z=W_{\mathrm{out}}h\]

for the entire vocabulary at every prediction step. The research team notices that most tokens are extremely rare, while a small subset accounts for the majority of observed predictions. You are asked to design an output architecture that exploits this imbalance without destroying the mathematical validity of the probability distribution.

Technical setup

Partition the vocabulary into:

A head containing (H=10,000) frequent tokens.

(C=10) tail clusters.

Each tail cluster contains approximately (99,000) tokens.

The total vocabulary size is:

\[V=H+C(99,000)=1,000,000.\]

For a hidden state (h), the architecture first computes a probability distribution over:

The 10,000 frequent tokens.

The 10 tail clusters.

The head distribution is:

\[P_{\mathrm{head}}(j\mid h).\]

For a token (w) belonging to tail cluster (c), the final probability is:

P{\mathrm{head}}(c\mid h) P{\mathrm{tail}}(w\mid c,h). ]

Research challenges

  • Show that the resulting vocabulary distribution is normalized if the head and each conditional tail distribution are individually normalized.
  • Derive the negative log-likelihood for a frequent token.
  • Derive the negative log-likelihood for a token belonging to a tail cluster.
  • Explain how the output computation differs between frequent and rare tokens.
  • Compare the computational complexity of the hierarchical architecture with a standard full-vocabulary projection.
  • Suppose the target token frequencies follow a highly imbalanced distribution. Why might the expected computation per prediction decrease substantially?
  • Explain why clustering the vocabulary incorrectly can make the architecture less efficient.
  • Suppose semantically related tokens are placed in different clusters. What difficulties might this introduce for the learned output distribution?
  • Compare hierarchical softmax with adaptive softmax and explain the different ways they structure the output computation.
  • Discuss the trade-off between reducing expected inference computation and adding additional conditional decisions to the output model.
  • How would multilingual vocabulary imbalance influence the design of the frequent-token head and tail clusters?
  • Design an experiment comparing full softmax, adaptive softmax, and hierarchical softmax using perplexity, inference latency, memory, and rare-token accuracy.

Hints

A tail-token probability is the product of a cluster-selection probability and a conditional within-cluster probability.

Expected computational cost depends on token frequency, not only on the total number of possible vocabulary entries.

SET 11 / EXERCISE 10

Exercise 10 — Building a Transformer That Does Not Care About the Order of Its Inputs

Domain: Set Transformers · Permutation equivariance · Permutation-invariant architectures

Core intuition: Standard self-attention without positional information is permutation equivariant, and an appropriate pooling operation can turn it into a permutation-invariant model for unordered data.

Scenario

A research group develops a Transformer for analyzing collections of scientific measurements. Each sample contains a variable number of observations, but the observations do not have a meaningful sequence order. For example, one sample might contain:

12 sensor measurements.

4 environmental measurements.

8 chemical measurements.

The current Transformer assigns different predictions when the same collection is presented in a different order. The researchers realize that the architecture is implicitly treating an unordered set as a sequence. You are asked to redesign it so that its output does not depend on arbitrary input ordering.

Technical setup

Let the input set be:

\[X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}.\]

Consider a permutation matrix:

\[P\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}.\]

Permuting the input elements produces:

\[X'=PX.\]

Define self-attention without positional encodings:

\operatorname{softmax} \left( \frac{XW_Q(XW_K)^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} \right) XW_V. ] All attention projections are shared across positions.

Research challenges

  • Prove that:
  • P\operatorname{Attn}(X).
  • Explain why this property is called permutation equivariance rather than permutation invariance.
  • Show why applying a standard position-wise feed-forward network preserves permutation equivariance.
  • Suppose a stack of such Transformer blocks is applied. Explain why the entire encoder remains permutation equivariant.
  • Consider mean pooling: \[z=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}h_i.\]
  • Prove that the pooled representation is permutation invariant.
  • Explain the difference between mean pooling, sum pooling, and max pooling when the number of input elements varies.
  • Suppose a learned classification token attends to all input elements but receives no positional embedding. Explain how it can produce a permutation-invariant output.
  • What happens to permutation symmetry when absolute positional embeddings are added to the input?
  • Some unordered datasets contain different types of elements, such as images, sensor records, and metadata. How could type embeddings preserve the distinction between element categories without imposing an arbitrary ordering?
  • Explain how padding and attention masks must be handled to preserve permutation symmetry over valid elements.
  • Compare a set-based Transformer with a conventional sequence Transformer for tasks in which ordering is either meaningful or irrelevant.
  • Design an experiment that randomly permutes inputs during evaluation and measures whether the architecture preserves its prediction.

Hints

A permutation reorders the rows of the input and the corresponding rows of the output.

The attention matrix changes under permutation, but its mathematical relationship to the value matrix remains consistent.

End of Problem Set 11

Transformer architecture research map

#

Research territory

Main design capability

01 Residual and normalization topology Designing extremely deep Transformers

02 Attention-head allocation Balancing independent attention patterns and head capacity
