Evidence support and factual truth are related but distinct evaluation questions.

SET 14 / EXERCISE 04

Exercise 04 — The Benchmark That Rewards Memorizing the Format Instead of Solving the Problem

Domain: Construct validity · Item response theory · Measurement invariance

Core intuition: A benchmark score is meaningful only if the evaluation items measure the capability researchers claim to measure.

Scenario

A laboratory evaluates two language models using a mathematical reasoning benchmark. Model A achieves 90%. Model B achieves 84%. The laboratory declares Model A superior. However, an external evaluator discovers that the benchmark questions follow a highly repetitive template. Model A may have learned the benchmark's formatting conventions, while Model B performs better on unfamiliar mathematical problems. You are asked to determine whether the benchmark genuinely measures mathematical reasoning.

Technical setup

Consider a two-parameter logistic item-response model:

\sigma\left(a_i(\theta_j-b_i)\right), ] where:

(X_{ij}) indicates whether model (j) answers item (i) correctly.

(\theta_j) represents the latent capability of model (j).

(a_i) represents item discrimination.

(b_i) represents item difficulty.

Consider two models with estimated capabilities:

\[\theta_A=1.0,\qquad\ \theta_B=0.8.\]

The benchmark contains:

20 easy items with (a=1,b=-1).

20 difficult items with (a=1,b=1).

A second benchmark contains 40 items with difficulty:

\[b=0.\]

Research challenges

  • Calculate the predicted success probability of both models on an easy item and a difficult item.
  • Derive the expected overall benchmark accuracy under the first benchmark.
  • Calculate the expected accuracy under the second benchmark.
  • Explain why benchmark composition influences observed model rankings when models have different capability profiles.
  • What does the discrimination parameter (a_i) represent? Why are low-discrimination items less informative about model ability?
  • Explain why the latent ability scale in an item-response model is not uniquely determined without a reference convention or anchor constraints.
  • Suppose the same item becomes substantially easier for one model family because it recognizes a familiar template. Why does this challenge the assumption that the item measures the same underlying capability for every model?
  • Explain measurement invariance and differential item functioning in the context of evaluating different language models.
  • Design a benchmark with separate dimensions for mathematical reasoning, symbolic manipulation, instruction following, and generalization.
  • Why should benchmark items contain controlled variations in surface form and underlying reasoning structure?
  • Discuss the difference between measuring a model's absolute ability and measuring its ability relative to a particular test population.
  • Design an evaluation procedure that investigates whether model rankings remain stable when benchmark difficulty and item composition change.

Hints

Benchmark accuracy is not a universal measure of capability.

A test item is informative only if it distinguishes between the ability levels researchers want to measure.

SET 14 / EXERCISE 05

Exercise 05 — The Model That Gives Different Answers to the Same Question

Domain: Metamorphic testing · Paraphrase robustness · Semantic invariance

Core intuition: A model should not change its substantive answer when irrelevant changes are made to the wording or formatting of a question.

Scenario

An AI assistant answers mathematical and scientific questions. A research team evaluates it using a fixed collection of prompts. The model achieves 95% accuracy. However, when the same questions are rephrased, accuracy falls to 71%. The engineering team argues that the new prompts are simply harder. You suspect that some differences are semantically irrelevant and should not alter the expected answer. You propose metamorphic testing.

Technical setup

Let:

\[q\]

represent an original task. Let:

\[\mathcal T(q)={q_1,\ldots,q_m}\]

be a collection of transformations that are intended to preserve the task's meaning. Examples include:

Rephrasing the question.

Changing the order of irrelevant contextual sentences.

Modifying punctuation.

Replacing variable names while preserving mathematical relationships.

Changing a table into an equivalent textual description.

Let:

\[f(q)\]

denote the model's response, and let:

\[g(f(q))\]

extract a task-relevant canonical answer. Define task accuracy:

\[A=\ \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^{N}\ \mathbf1(g(f(q_i))=y_i).\]

Define within-group answer consistency:

\cdots g(f(q_{i,m})) \right). ]

Research challenges

  • Explain the difference between semantic equivalence and superficial textual similarity.
  • Construct a pair of prompts that differ substantially in wording but require exactly the same mathematical answer.
  • Construct a pair of prompts that look almost identical but have different correct answers because of one altered condition.
  • Explain why a robustness test must distinguish genuinely meaning-preserving transformations from transformations that change the task.
  • Calculate accuracy and consistency for an evaluation set in which 100 base problems each have five equivalent variants, and 420 out of 500 responses are correct.
  • Suppose a model answers every paraphrased problem identically but is wrong on every version. Why is consistency alone an inadequate evaluation metric?
  • Define a joint metric that accounts for both task correctness and answer consistency.
  • Explain why prompt-format sensitivity can reveal hidden dependencies on training conventions rather than genuine task understanding.
  • Design a factorial evaluation that varies mathematical notation, sentence order, irrelevant context, and variable naming independently.
  • How could response randomness interfere with the interpretation of paraphrase sensitivity?
  • Explain how multiple independent model samples per prompt can help distinguish semantic sensitivity from decoding variability.
  • Propose an evaluation report that presents accuracy, consistency, and worst-case degradation under meaning-preserving transformations.

Hints

Correctness and invariance should be measured separately.

A transformation is suitable only when it preserves the intended problem, not merely its topic.

SET 14 / EXERCISE 06

Exercise 06 — The Assistant That Remembers an Old Decision and Ignores the New One

Domain: Multi-turn evaluation · State tracking · Conversational consistency · Temporal reasoning

Core intuition: A model's ability to answer individual questions does not guarantee that it can maintain a correct evolving state across a long conversation.

Scenario

A company deploys an AI assistant that helps research teams manage experiments. Over several conversations, the user specifies:

The project name.

The current dataset version.

The active evaluation metric.

The intended model architecture.

Several changes to these decisions.

The assistant answers individual questions correctly most of the time. However, it occasionally uses an outdated dataset version or continues following a decision that the user explicitly replaced. The engineering team claims that the model has enough context because all messages are present in its conversation history. You are asked to design a rigorous state-tracking evaluation.

Technical setup

Represent the conversational state at time (t) as:

\[S_t=\ (v_t^{(1)},v_t^{(2)},\ldots,v_t^{(K)}),\]

where each component represents a maintained fact or decision. A message (m_t) induces a state transition:

\[St=F(S{t-1},m_t).\]

Consider the following interaction:

Dataset version is established as (v_1). Evaluation metric is established as MSE. Dataset version is changed to (v_2). An unrelated discussion of five other topics occurs. The evaluation metric is changed to MAE. The user asks which dataset version and metric are currently active.

The correct state is:

\[S_{\mathrm{final}}=(v_2,\mathrm{MAE}).\]

Research challenges

  • Formalize the sequence of state transitions.
  • Explain why retrieving every earlier message is not sufficient to guarantee correct state reconstruction.
  • Define exact state accuracy for a model maintaining (K) independent state variables.
  • Suppose the model correctly retrieves 18 out of 20 state variables. Calculate state accuracy.
  • Explain why exact-match evaluation can be stricter than semantic state equivalence.
  • Construct a test in which an old decision and its replacement appear far apart in the conversation.
  • Construct a test in which the user explicitly revokes a previous instruction without providing a replacement.
  • Distinguish errors caused by:
  • Failure to locate the relevant message.
  • Failure to identify which message is most recent.
  • Failure to interpret the update correctly.
  • Failure to maintain the state across unrelated discussions.
  • Define a stale-state error rate measuring how often the assistant uses an invalidated value.
  • Explain how distractor messages and repeated discussions can affect state reconstruction.
  • Design an evaluation that separately varies context length, update distance, number of revisions, and number of unrelated messages.
  • Propose an automated state ledger or structured memory interface and explain what new failure modes it might introduce.

Hints

The latest valid state is not necessarily the first mention, the most frequent mention, or the most detailed mention.

Distinguish conversation retrieval from temporal update resolution.

SET 14 / EXERCISE 07

Exercise 07 — The Model That Looks Robust Until One Small Change Is Introduced at a Time

Domain: Robustness testing · Factorial experiments · Interaction effects

Core intuition: Evaluating input perturbations independently can miss failure modes that appear only when several small changes occur together.

Scenario

A research laboratory evaluates a Transformer-based document-understanding system. It tests robustness to:

OCR errors.

Missing punctuation.

Whitespace changes.

Unicode normalization.

Minor spelling mistakes.

The model performs well under every individual transformation. However, real documents often contain several of these imperfections simultaneously. When the team evaluates combinations of transformations, performance deteriorates sharply. You suspect the evaluation procedure has underestimated interaction effects.

Technical setup

Consider four binary input conditions:

(A): OCR corruption present.

(B): Punctuation altered.

(C): Unicode normalization changed.

(D): Whitespace corruption present.

Let the model's performance be:

\[Y(A,B,C,D).\]

A simple additive model would be:

\beta_0 +\beta_AA +\beta_BB +\beta_CC +\beta_DD +\epsilon. ] However, a more general factorial model includes interaction terms: \beta0 +\sum_i\beta_iX_i +\sum{i&#x3C;j}\beta_{ij}X_iX_j +\epsilon. ]

Research challenges

  • Explain why testing each corruption independently cannot reveal all possible combinations of input failures.
  • Calculate the number of possible experimental conditions under a complete four-factor binary factorial design.
  • Explain the meaning of a two-factor interaction coefficient such as: \[\beta_{AB}.\]
  • Suppose OCR corruption alone reduces accuracy by 2 percentage points and punctuation alteration alone reduces accuracy by 1 percentage point.
  • How would you detect whether their combination causes an additional 10-percentage-point degradation?
  • Construct a response table for a simplified two-factor experiment and calculate the interaction effect.
  • Explain why a model can appear robust to each individual perturbation while remaining fragile to their combination.
  • Compare full factorial testing with fractional factorial testing. What information can be lost when using a reduced experimental design?
  • Suppose the four corruption conditions have different real-world frequencies. Why might equally weighting every factorial condition produce an evaluation that does not represent production risk?
  • Define a robustness degradation curve as perturbation severity increases.
  • Explain how to distinguish benign perturbations that preserve meaning from modifications that genuinely change the task.
  • Design a risk-weighted evaluation combining corruption severity, occurrence probability, and failure consequence.
  • Propose an experiment investigating whether a new Transformer preprocessing pipeline reduces interaction effects rather than merely improving average accuracy.

Hints

The total effect of two simultaneous perturbations is not necessarily the sum of their individual effects.

Factorial experiments are specifically designed to reveal interactions.

SET 14 / EXERCISE 08

Exercise 08 — The Attack That Is Hidden Inside a Document the Model Was Asked to Summarize

Domain: Prompt injection · Trust boundaries · Instruction hierarchy · Security evaluation

Core intuition: A model must distinguish instructions that define its task from untrusted content that it is merely supposed to process.

Scenario

An enterprise deploys a Transformer assistant that reads documents, emails, and research reports. Employees ask it to summarize documents and extract relevant information. An external document occasionally contains text that attempts to redirect the assistant away from its intended task. The assistant sometimes follows the embedded instructions rather than treating them as document content. The engineering team argues that the model should simply become better at instruction following. You argue that the central problem is not ordinary instruction following but the architecture and policy used to distinguish trusted instructions from untrusted data.

Technical setup

Consider an assistant with three conceptual input regions:

\[X=(S,U,D),\]

where:

(S): trusted system-level instructions.

(U): trusted user request.

(D): untrusted external document content.

The desired behavior is:

\[Y=f(S,U,D)\]

subject to the requirement that the document content is analyzed as data and does not acquire the authority of a trusted instruction. Define attack success rate: \frac{\text{number of successful unauthorized task deviations}} {\text{number of attack evaluations}}. ] Also define benign task accuracy: \frac{\text{correct benign responses}} {\text{benign evaluations}}. ]

Research challenges

  • Explain why treating all text in the context window as equally authoritative creates a security problem.
  • Distinguish direct prompt injection from indirect prompt injection.
  • Give an abstract example in which an external document contains malicious instructions but the correct behavior is to summarize them as content rather than execute them.
  • Design a benchmark containing benign documents, maliciously crafted documents, and ambiguous documents.
  • Calculate ASR if 17 out of 200 attack trials cause unauthorized task deviations.
  • Suppose a defensive modification reduces ASR but also reduces benign task accuracy from 96% to 78%. Explain why this is not automatically an acceptable improvement.
  • Define a joint security-utility evaluation that accounts for both attack success and unnecessary refusal.
  • Explain why evaluating only static attack examples can overestimate robustness against adaptive attackers.
  • Design a defense-in-depth architecture that separates trusted instructions, untrusted document content, tool outputs, and authorized actions.
  • Discuss the limitations of relying exclusively on explicit textual delimiters to establish trust boundaries.
  • Suppose the assistant can call external tools. Why should authorization checks occur outside the language model's generated text?
  • Design a red-team evaluation that tests direct, indirect, multi-turn, and cross-tool injection scenarios while avoiding reliance on one fixed attack template.

Hints

Content can be relevant to a task without possessing authority over how the task is performed.

Security should not depend entirely on the model correctly interpreting arbitrary text as trustworthy or untrustworthy.

SET 14 / EXERCISE 09

Exercise 09 — The Model That Passes Every Component Test but Still Fails in Production

Domain: Reliability engineering · Fault trees · System-level evaluation · Failure dependencies

Core intuition: End-to-end system reliability depends on the interaction of components, and component-level success rates cannot simply be multiplied unless the dependence assumptions are justified.

Scenario

A company deploys a Transformer-based research assistant. Its inference pipeline includes:

Input preprocessing. Context construction. Model generation. Output validation.

Each component passes its individual evaluation. However, end-to-end task completion remains substantially below expectations. The engineering team argues that every component is reliable and therefore the overall system must be reliable. You are asked to investigate system-level reliability and failure propagation.

Technical setup

Let the component-success events be:

\[E_1,E_2,E_3,E_4.\]

The complete system succeeds only if every component succeeds:

E_1\cap E_2\cap E_3\cap E_4. ] Suppose the marginal component success probabilities are:

\[P(E_1)=0.995,\]

\[P(E_2)=0.990,\]

\[P(E_3)=0.980,\]

\[P(E_4)=0.995.\]

If component successes are independent:

\prod_{i=1}^{4}P(E_i). ] Without independence, the chain rule gives: P(E_1) P(E_2\mid E_1) P(E_3\mid E_1,E_2) P(E_4\mid E_1,E_2,E_3). ]

Research challenges

  • Calculate the end-to-end success probability under the independence assumption.
  • Calculate the corresponding end-to-end failure probability.
  • Explain why four individually reliable components can produce a noticeably less reliable complete system.
  • Prove the general chain-rule expression for system success.
  • Explain why multiplying marginal success probabilities is invalid when component failures are dependent.
  • Consider the union bound: \[P(E{\mathrm{system}}^c) \ \leq \ \sum{i=1}^{4}P(E_i^c).\]
  • Derive a lower bound on system success that does not require independence.
  • Compare the independence estimate with the dependence-free bound.
  • Construct a scenario in which failure in the preprocessing stage increases the probability of failure in context construction.
  • Explain how common-cause failures can invalidate independent component reliability assumptions.
  • Construct a fault tree for a system in which task failure can occur through several alternative failure paths.
  • Distinguish component accuracy, conditional component reliability, and end-to-end task success.
  • Propose a fault-injection evaluation that deliberately introduces preprocessing errors, missing context, generation errors, and validation failures.
  • Explain why improving the weakest component is not always the most effective way to improve overall reliability when failures are strongly dependent.

Hints

Component reliability is not automatically system reliability.

A failure in one stage may change the input conditions and therefore the probability of failure in later stages.

SET 14 / EXERCISE 10

Exercise 10 — The Model Update That Improves the Average Score but Makes a Minority of Users Worse Off

Domain: Regression testing · Subgroup evaluation · Non-inferiority analysis · Paired experiments

Core intuition: A model update can improve overall performance while causing serious regressions in specific populations or task categories, so release evaluation must consider both average improvement and subgroup harm.

Scenario

A company releases a new version of a language model. On its main benchmark, accuracy improves from 86% to 89%. The research team announces a successful upgrade. However, users report that the new model is substantially worse at several specific tasks, particularly scientific notation and multilingual mathematical questions. The engineering team argues that the improvement in average accuracy justifies the update. You are asked to design a more rigorous release-evaluation protocol.

Technical setup

The old and new models are evaluated on the same 10,000 benchmark examples. The population is divided into four predefined subgroups:

Group Number of examples Old-model accuracy New-model accuracy

General questions 5,000 90% 93%

Mathematical reasoning 2,000 85% 87%

Scientific notation 1,000 88% 75%

Multilingual reasoning 2,000 75% 80%

Define:

A_{\mathrm{new},g} A_{\mathrm{old},g}. ] The release team also uses a paired comparison because both models are evaluated on the same examples. Define:

(n_{01}): examples where the old model is wrong and the new model is correct.

(n_{10}): examples where the old model is correct and the new model is wrong.

McNemar's statistic, with a continuity correction, is:

\frac{(|n{01}-n{10}|-1)^2} {n{01}+n{10}}. ]

Research challenges

  • Calculate the overall accuracy of both models.
  • Calculate the absolute and relative accuracy improvement for each subgroup.
  • Explain how the large general-question subgroup can conceal a serious regression in scientific notation.
  • Calculate the weighted overall change using the subgroup sample proportions.
  • Define a worst-group performance metric:
  • \min_g A_g.
  • Compare the old and new models under this metric.
  • Explain why aggregate benchmark accuracy and worst-group accuracy answer different questions.
  • Under what circumstances is a paired comparison statistically more informative than comparing two independent accuracy estimates?
  • Construct an example of paired outcomes where two models have identical accuracy but differ substantially in which examples they answer correctly.
  • Explain the purpose of McNemar's test and identify the observations that contribute directly to its statistic.
  • Suppose the release team defines a maximum acceptable subgroup degradation of: \[\delta=0.03.\]
  • Formulate a non-inferiority requirement for each critical subgroup.
  • Why should the team predefine critical subgroups before inspecting the results rather than selecting only favorable subgroup definitions afterward?
  • Discuss the multiple-comparison problem when testing dozens of subgroups.
  • Design a release gate that combines:
  • Overall performance.
  • Worst-group performance.
  • Critical subgroup non-inferiority.
  • Paired statistical evidence.
  • Severity-weighted failure analysis.
  • Explain why a release decision should distinguish genuine improvements from regressions that are unacceptable even when the aggregate benchmark increases.

Hints

Compare the two models on the same individual examples, not just their final percentages.

Average performance is a weighted summary; it does not guarantee that every subgroup benefits.

End of Problem Set 14

Transformer evaluation and reliability research map

#

Research territory

Main research capability

01 Benchmark contamination Auditing evaluation independence

02 LLM-as-a-judge Detecting evaluator bias

03 Claim-level factuality Measuring evidence support and factual errors

04 Construct validity and IRT Determining whether benchmarks measure actual capabilities

05 Metamorphic testing Evaluating semantic consistency across equivalent prompts

06 Conversational state evaluation Testing temporal consistency and memory updates

07 Factorial robustness testing Detecting interactions between input corruptions

08 Prompt-injection security Evaluating trust boundaries and instruction integrity

09 Reliability engineering Understanding end-to-end system failures

10 Regression testing Detecting subgroup degradation during model upgrades

Final examination standard

Every exercise should produce five distinct forms of analysis.

  1. Evaluation specification

Define exactly what capability or failure mechanism is being measured.

  1. Mathematical formulation

Derive the relevant probabilities, metrics, reliability relationships, or statistical comparisons.

  1. Failure investigation

Identify how an apparently successful model or evaluation protocol can produce misleading conclusions.

  1. Experimental design

Develop controlled tests that isolate the suspected source of failure.

  1. Deployment judgment

Determine what evidence is sufficient to trust the model, reject an update, or require further investigation.

The ultimate research challenge

Imagine that a company tells you:

"Our latest Transformer is state-of-the-art. It beats every competitor, passes our safety tests, and achieves 95% accuracy." You are responsible for auditing that claim. Can you establish:

Whether its benchmark was contaminated?

Whether the evaluator was biased?

Whether its factual claims are supported?

Whether its test actually measures the intended capability?

Whether harmless prompt changes alter its behavior?

Whether it maintains correct state across conversations?

Whether multiple small corruptions cause unexpected failures?

Whether untrusted content can redirect its behavior?

Whether the complete system is reliable?

Whether its latest update has harmed a minority of users?

The objective is to become the researcher who does not merely ask whether a Transformer performs well, but can establish exactly what its performance means, where its guarantees end, and what evidence is still missing.

Mechanistic InterpretabilityCOLLECTION 15 / 15

Problem Set 15 — Inside the Transformer: Mechanistic Interpretability

Discovering Circuits, Features, Internal Memories, and Causal Computations

Difficulty: Advanced Graduate → Early PhD

Central objective: Develop the ability to reverse-engineer Transformer computations, identify internal representations, understand how individual components cooperate, and establish whether a proposed mechanistic explanation is scientifically justified.

General instructions

You are an independent mechanistic interpretability researcher investigating a pretrained Transformer. You are not interested merely in knowing which attention head activates or which neuron has a large activation. You want to understand what computation the model performs, how information travels through its internal architecture, and which components are responsible for specific behaviors. For every exercise:

Reconstruct the relevant internal mechanism mathematically. Identify the representations and transformations involved. Distinguish correlations from causal contributions. Investigate alternative explanations. Construct falsifiable hypotheses. Design experiments that could validate or reject your proposed mechanism.

No coding is required. No solutions are provided.

SET 15 / EXERCISE 01

Exercise 01 — The Attention Head That Predicts the Next Token by Remembering the Previous Appearance of the Current Token

Domain: Induction heads · Attention circuits · In-context learning

Core intuition: A Transformer can implement a simple associative retrieval mechanism by composing two attention heads, allowing it to recognize repeated sequence patterns and predict what follows them.

Scenario

You are investigating a language model that performs surprisingly well on sequences containing repeated patterns. Consider: "The researcher opened the door, examined the laboratory, and returned to the researcher..." The model appears to recognize that an earlier occurrence of "the researcher" was followed by information that may now be relevant. You suspect that an internal circuit has learned to identify previous occurrences of a token and retrieve what followed them. You want to understand whether this behavior can emerge from the composition of two relatively simple attention heads.

Technical setup

Consider the token sequence:

\[[A,B,C,A\]

] The desired next-token prediction is:

\[B.\]

Introduce two idealized attention heads. Head 1 — Previous-token head At position (j), this head writes a representation of the previous token into the residual stream. Represent its output using:

\[pj=e{x_{j-1}},\]

where (e{x{j-1}}) is the embedding of the preceding token. For the first position, define a special null representation. Head 2 — Induction head At the current position (t), its query identifies the current token:

\[qt=e{x_t}.\]

At an earlier candidate position (j), its key contains the previous-token representation:

\[kj=e{x_{j-1}}.\]

Its attention scores are:

\frac{q_t^\top k_j}{\tau}. ] Its values retrieve the token at the candidate position:

\[vj=e{x_j}.\]

The attention output is:

\[ot=\sum{j&#x3C;t}\ \operatorname{softmax}(s_{tj})v_j.\]

Assume token embeddings are orthonormal and the temperature is chosen so that matching positions receive much larger scores than nonmatching positions.

Research challenges

  • At position (t=4), identify the earlier position whose key matches the query.
  • Determine which token is retrieved from the value associated with that position.
  • Explain how the first head transforms the original sequence into information that the second head can use.
  • Derive the attention score for matching and nonmatching token identities under the orthonormal embedding assumption.
  • In the limit of increasingly sharp attention, determine the resulting attention output.
  • Suppose the sequence becomes: \[[A,B,C,A,D,A\]
  • At the final position, which earlier occurrences are candidates for induction? Explain how a recency preference could distinguish them.
  • What happens when the same token appears several times but is followed by different tokens? Why can induction become ambiguous?
  • Suppose the first head writes the previous-token representation into the residual stream, but the second head's key projection cannot extract it. Explain why the circuit breaks despite the presence of both heads.
  • Explain how the value projection converts retrieved contextual information into a direction that can influence the next-token distribution.
  • Why can induction-like behavior emerge as a circuit-level computation rather than being implemented by one isolated attention head?
  • Design an experiment using repeated-token sequences with controlled patterns to determine whether an identified pair of heads implements induction-like behavior.
  • Propose a test that distinguishes genuine pattern retrieval from a simpler heuristic that favors frequent or recently observed tokens.

Hints

The important information at an earlier candidate position is not only the token located there, but also the token that preceded it.

One component constructs an associative key; another uses that key to retrieve the corresponding value.

SET 15 / EXERCISE 02

Exercise 02 — The MLP That Behaves Like a Database Stored Inside the Neural Network

Domain: MLP key-value memories · Feed-forward layers · Associative representations

Core intuition: A Transformer feed-forward network can store associations between input features and output features, functioning approximately like a distributed associative memory.

Scenario

You are investigating how a Transformer stores factual associations. You discover that certain factual relationships appear to be retrieved through its feed-forward layers. For example:

A key representing a particular subject.

A value representing an associated property.

An input context that activates the corresponding internal transformation.

The research team proposes that an MLP can be interpreted as a collection of key-value memories. You are asked to determine when this interpretation is mathematically reasonable.

Technical setup

Consider a two-layer MLP:

\[f(x)=W{\mathrm{out}}\ \operatorname{ReLU}(W{\mathrm{in}}x+b{\mathrm{in}})\ +b{\mathrm{out}}.\]

Let:

\[W_{\mathrm{in}}\in\mathbb R^{m\times d},\]

\[W_{\mathrm{out}}\in\mathbb R^{d\times m}.\]

For hidden neuron (j), define:

\[kj^\top=(W{\mathrm{in}})_{j,:}\]

and:

\[vj=(W{\mathrm{out}})_{:,j}.\]

The activation of neuron (j) is:

\[a_j(x)=\ \operatorname{ReLU}(k_j^\top x+b_j).\]

Therefore:

\[f(x)=\sum{j=1}^{m}a_j(x)v_j+b{\mathrm{out}}.\]

Research challenges

  • Express the contribution of an individual hidden neuron to the MLP output.
  • Explain why (k_j) can be interpreted as an input feature detector and (v_j) as an output direction.
  • Suppose: \[k_1= \ \begin{pmatrix} \ 1\ \ 0 \ \end{pmatrix}, \ \qquad \ k_2= \ \begin{pmatrix} \ \cos\phi\ \ \sin\phi \ \end{pmatrix}.\]
  • For inputs aligned with each key, calculate the activation of both neurons as a function of (\phi), assuming zero biases.
  • Explain why two memories with highly correlated keys may activate simultaneously.
  • What happens when two neurons activate for similar inputs but write conflicting value directions?
  • Derive the Jacobian of the MLP in a region where its activation pattern is fixed.
  • Explain why the MLP behaves as a different linear transformation in different activation regions.
  • Suppose only one ReLU neuron is active for a particular input. Express the local transformation performed by that neuron.
  • Why can a single MLP contain many more potential input-output associations than the number of neurons alone might suggest?
  • Discuss the distinction between a literal key-value table and a distributed associative memory in which multiple neurons cooperate to represent one fact.
  • Design an experiment that systematically modifies the input key direction and measures the resulting output-value activation.
  • Propose a method for distinguishing factual associations stored in an MLP from associations produced primarily by surrounding attention context.

Hints

Each neuron contributes an outer-product-like transformation between an input detection direction and an output direction.

A memory can be partially activated by inputs that resemble its key without being identical to its original training pattern.

SET 15 / EXERCISE 03

Exercise 03 — Which Transformer Layer Actually Caused the Model to Predict a Word?

Domain: Residual-stream decomposition · Direct logit attribution · Computational attribution

Core intuition: Because Transformer layers write into a shared residual stream, individual components can contribute additively to final logits, allowing researchers to investigate where prediction-relevant information enters the computation.

Scenario

You investigate a language model that predicts the token "Paris" after reading:

"The capital of France is..." The engineering team claims that a particular attention head is responsible for predicting "Paris". However, the prediction could involve information written by token embeddings, multiple attention heads, and several MLP layers. You want to establish how much each component contributes directly to the final prediction.

Technical setup

For a simplified Transformer with additive residual updates:

\[rL=r_0+\sum{\ell=1}^{L}\Delta r_\ell,\]

where:

(r_0) contains the initial representation.

(\Delta r_\ell) represents the residual update from a component or layer.

Temporarily assume the final output transformation is linear:

\[z=W_Ur_L+b.\]

Here:

\[W_U\in\mathbb R^{V\times d}.\]

Let (u_t) denote the unembedding vector corresponding to vocabulary token (t). The logit for token (t) is:

\[z_t=u_t^\top r_L+b_t.\]

For a predicted token (a) and competing token (b), define the logit margin:

\[m_{a,b}=z_a-z_b.\]

Research challenges

  • Substitute the residual-stream decomposition into the final logit equation.
  • Prove that the pre-normalization logit can be expressed as the sum of contributions from the initial embedding and every residual update.
  • Derive the direct contribution of layer (\ell) to token (t)'s logit: \[c{\ell,t}=u_t^\top\Delta r\ell.\]
  • Derive the corresponding contribution to the logit margin between tokens (a) and (b).
  • Suppose one attention head writes a direction that increases the logit of "Paris" but also increases the logit of "London". Explain why analyzing its contribution to one logit alone can be misleading.
  • Construct a hypothetical example in which one layer contributes positively to the target token's logit while another contributes negatively.
  • Explain the difference between direct logit attribution and the total causal effect of a component after downstream layers have processed its output.
  • In a real Transformer, final LayerNorm is applied before the unembedding matrix. Why does this make the exact additive attribution problem more complicated?
  • Derive a first-order approximation to the change in the final logits produced by a small residual perturbation when the final normalization is present.
  • Explain why direct logit attribution is useful for generating hypotheses but does not independently establish that a component is necessary for the model's behavior.
  • Design a layer-wise attribution report that includes target logits, competing logits, and total logit margins.
  • Propose an experiment that compares direct logit attribution with controlled component ablation.

Hints

Decompose the residual stream before projecting it into vocabulary space.

A component's direct output contribution is not necessarily equal to its full downstream causal effect.

SET 15 / EXERCISE 04

Exercise 04 — When One Attention Head Writes Something Another Head Can Read

Domain: Attention composition · QK circuits · OV circuits · Head-to-head communication

Core intuition: Attention heads do not operate independently; their outputs modify the residual stream and can alter how later attention heads select information.

Scenario

You investigate a Transformer containing several attention heads. One head appears to detect a particular relationship between tokens and writes a feature into the residual stream. A later head appears to use that feature when calculating its own attention distribution. The research team wants to determine whether these two heads form a computational circuit. You are asked to analyze the composition mathematically.

Technical setup

Let the residual stream be:

\[X\in\mathbb R^{T\times d}.\]

Suppose attention head A produces:

P_AXW_V^AW_O^A, ] where:

(P_A\in\mathbb R^{T\times T}) is its attention matrix.

(W_V^A\in\mathbb R^{d\times d_v}).

(W_O^A\in\mathbb R^{d_v\times d}).

For this local analysis, treat the attention pattern (P_A) as fixed. The residual stream entering attention head B becomes:

\[X'=X+\Delta X_A.\]

Head B computes:

\[Q_B=X'W_Q^B,\ \qquad\ K_B=X'W_K^B.\]

Its attention-score matrix is:

\[S_B=\ \frac{Q_BK_B^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}.\]

Research challenges

  • Expand the attention-score matrix of head B after head A writes into the residual stream.
  • Separate the resulting expression into:
  • Original-input interactions.
  • Interactions involving the output of head A.
  • Interactions between the written representation at both query and key positions.
  • Explain how the product: \[W_V^AW_O^AW_Q^B\] can influence the query computation of head B.
  • Similarly, investigate how: \[W_V^AW_O^AW_K^B\] influences the key computation of head B.
  • Describe the conditions under which head A can write a feature that head B can reliably detect.
  • Suppose head A writes a feature direction orthogonal to the query and key readout directions of head B. What happens to the first-order communication pathway?
  • Explain the distinction between a QK circuit, which influences attention selection, and an OV circuit, which influences the information written through attention.
  • Construct a hypothetical example in which head A changes which token head B attends to without directly contributing the final semantic value retrieved by head B.
  • Why might independently analyzing the attention patterns of heads A and B fail to reveal their combined computational behavior?
  • Discuss how residual-stream interference from other heads can complicate the identification of a specific composition pathway.
  • Design an experiment that compares head B's attention scores before and after selectively removing the contribution of head A.
  • Propose an analysis distinguishing direct head-to-head composition from two heads independently responding to the same input feature.

Hints

Substitute the residual update into both the query and key equations.

The relevant mechanism is not simply whether two heads attend to similar tokens, but whether the output of one changes the computational behavior of the other.

SET 15 / EXERCISE 05

Exercise 05 — Why Does One Neuron Appear to Understand Mathematics, Geography, and Sentiment?

Domain: Feature superposition · Polysemantic neurons · Sparse feature geometry

Core intuition: A neuron is a coordinate in an internal representation space, not necessarily a single semantic feature; several features can be encoded in overlapping directions.

Scenario

You investigate a Transformer using activation analysis. One neuron appears to activate strongly for:

Mathematical expressions.

Geographical names.

Positive sentiment.

The researchers conclude that the neuron has learned an unusually broad semantic concept. You suspect that the neuron may instead be responding to several distinct features represented in a superposition. You decide to investigate how several feature directions can coexist within a lower-dimensional representation space.

Technical setup

Consider three unit feature directions in:

\[\mathbb R^2.\]

Define:

\[f_1=\ \begin{pmatrix}\ 1\\ 0\ \end{pmatrix},\]

\[f_2=\ \begin{pmatrix}\ -\frac12\\ \frac{\sqrt3}{2}\ \end{pmatrix},\]

\[f_3=\ \begin{pmatrix}\ -\frac12\\ -\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\ \end{pmatrix}.\]

Each representation is constructed as:

\[x=a_1f_1+a_2f_2+a_3f_3.\]

Assume the coefficients (a_i) are nonnegative feature activations and that only a small subset is usually active in any individual example.

Research challenges

  • Verify that the three feature vectors are normalized.
  • Calculate every pairwise inner product.
  • Explain why the three directions cannot be mutually orthogonal in a two-dimensional space.
  • Derive the projection of (x) onto each feature direction: \[f_i^\top x.\]
  • Suppose only feature 1 is active. What does a simple projection-based decoder recover?
  • Suppose features 1 and 2 are simultaneously active. Calculate the interference term appearing in the projection onto (f_1).
  • Suppose all three features have equal activation. Determine the resulting representation vector.
  • Explain why the activation pattern and feature co-occurrence distribution are crucial for determining whether superposition is useful or harmful.
  • Distinguish a neuron from a feature direction. Why can one neuron participate in representing multiple underlying features?
  • Explain how a sparse autoencoder can attempt to recover a larger collection of feature directions from a lower-dimensional residual stream.
  • Why does identifying a feature that activates on certain examples not automatically prove that the feature represents the associated semantic concept?
  • Design an experiment that tests feature selectivity across systematically varied mathematical, geographical, and sentiment-related inputs.
  • Discuss the potential interpretability trade-offs between representing many features through superposition and allocating dedicated dimensions to individual features.

Hints

Feature geometry and neuron identity are not the same thing.

Sparse activation patterns can make overlapping feature directions more distinguishable than their raw geometric overlap might suggest.

SET 15 / EXERCISE 06

Exercise 06 — Can You Read What a Transformer Knows Before Its Final Layer?

Domain: Logit lens · Tuned lens · Intermediate representations · Layer-wise prediction analysis

Core intuition: Intermediate residual representations can be projected into vocabulary space to investigate how predictions develop throughout the network, but an intermediate prediction is not necessarily the model's final computational decision.

Scenario

A language model receives:

"The largest planet in our solar system is..." You suspect that the model begins constructing the prediction "Jupiter" well before its final layer. The research team wants to investigate where this information first becomes visible. You propose applying the final vocabulary projection to intermediate residual-stream representations. However, another researcher argues that intermediate layers may not yet use the same representation geometry as the final layer. You are asked to compare the ordinary logit lens with a learned tuned lens.

Technical setup

Let:

\[r_0,r_1,\ldots,r_L\]

denote residual-stream representations at successive layers. The final model logits are:

\[z_L=W_U\operatorname{LN}_f(r_L)+b.\]

Here, (W_U) is the unembedding matrix and (\operatorname{LN}_f) denotes the final normalization. The logit lens at layer (\ell) is: WU\operatorname{LN}_f(r\ell)+b. ] For a tuned lens, introduce a layer-specific affine translator:

\[T\ell(r\ell)=A\ell r\ell+c_\ell.\]

The tuned-lens logits are:

WU\operatorname{LN}_f(T\ell(r_\ell))+b. ] A possible training objective for the translator is: D{\mathrm{KL}} \left( P_L|P\ell^{\mathrm{TL}} \right), ] where both distributions are obtained using softmax over their corresponding logits.

Research challenges

  • Explain how an intermediate residual-stream vector can be converted into a vocabulary distribution.
  • Calculate the conceptual difference between reusing the final unembedding directly and learning a layer-specific affine translator.
  • Why might the ordinary logit lens produce misleading predictions at early layers?
  • Explain why the residual stream may contain information that is not yet expressed in a coordinate system directly aligned with the final vocabulary projection.
  • Derive the KL-divergence objective for training a tuned lens at one layer.
  • Explain why minimizing this KL divergence encourages the intermediate distribution to resemble the final model distribution.
  • Suppose the logit lens predicts "Jupiter" at layer 5 but the tuned lens predicts "gas giant" at that layer. How could these differing predictions reflect different aspects of intermediate representation geometry?
  • Distinguish a layer that contains information about the final answer from a layer that has completed the computation required to produce that answer.
  • Suppose an intermediate layer predicts the correct token with high probability, but the final model predicts another token. What possible computational explanations should be investigated?
  • Why can an affine translator improve interpretability without proving that the translated representation is actually used by the original model?
  • Explain how entropy and top-token probability can be tracked across layers to investigate the evolution of predictive certainty.
  • Design an experiment comparing ordinary logit lens and tuned lens across several layers, token categories, and prompt types.
  • Identify the limitations of interpreting intermediate vocabulary predictions as direct evidence of when the model has "decided" on an answer.

Hints

A representation may contain useful information before it is aligned with the final output coordinate system.

Predictive readability and actual computational causality are different properties.

SET 15 / EXERCISE 07

Exercise 07 — The Token That Receives Attention Without Contributing Almost Anything

Domain: Attention sinks · Softmax normalization · Residual-stream dynamics

Core intuition: An attention head can allocate substantial probability mass to a token that contributes little semantic information, because attention probabilities also control how the remaining value vectors are weighted.

Scenario

You inspect the attention patterns of a language model. Across long sequences, an early token repeatedly receives a large fraction of attention from many later positions. However, its content appears semantically irrelevant to the prediction. The research team concludes that the model must have learned an important long-range dependency involving that token. You suspect that this interpretation may be incorrect. You hypothesize that the token functions as an attention sink: it absorbs attention probability while contributing relatively little information to the output.

Technical setup

For one attention query, suppose there is:

One sink token with score (s_0) and value (v_0).

(K) ordinary content tokens with scores (s_1,\ldots,s_K) and values (v_1,\ldots,v_K).

Define the ordinary content-only partition function:

\[Z=\sum_{i=1}^{K}e^{s_i}.\]

The full attention output is:

\[o=\ \frac{\ e^{s0}v_0+\sum{i=1}^{K}e^{s_i}v_i\ }{\ e^{s_0}+Z\ }.\]

Consider the special case:

\[v_0=0.\]

Define the content-only attention output:

\frac1Z \sum_{i=1}^{K}e^{s_i}v_i. ]

Research challenges

  • Express the sink attention probability in terms of (s_0) and (Z).
  • Derive the relationship between the ordinary content-token attention probabilities and their probabilities after introducing the sink.
  • Prove that when (v_0=0), the full attention output is a scaled version of the content-only output.
  • Explain how increasing (s_0) changes the magnitude of the resulting attention output even though the sink contributes no direct value vector.
  • Suppose: \[Z=10,\qquad s_0=\log 10.\]
  • Calculate the total attention probability assigned to the sink.
  • What happens to the content attention mass when the sink score becomes much larger than the content logits?
  • Explain why attention probability alone is insufficient for identifying which token contributes meaningful information to the residual stream.
  • Suppose the sink value vector is small but nonzero. Derive the resulting output as a combination of the sink contribution and the scaled content contribution.
  • Discuss how an attention sink could help regulate output magnitude or provide a stable destination for attention that would otherwise be distributed across content tokens.
  • Explain why removing a sink token may change model behavior even when that token carries little direct semantic information.
  • Design an experiment comparing attention weights, value-vector magnitudes, and output-projection contributions for candidate sink tokens.
  • Propose a method for distinguishing genuine long-range information retrieval from attention used primarily for normalization or residual-output control.

Hints

Attention weights determine how values are mixed, but the size and direction of each value also matter.

Analyze the denominator of softmax, not just the content of the token receiving attention.

SET 15 / EXERCISE 08

Exercise 08 — Adding One Direction to the Residual Stream and Changing What the Model Says

Domain: Activation steering · Representation intervention · Linear control directions

Core intuition: A carefully selected direction in activation space can systematically alter model behavior, but finding a direction correlated with a concept does not guarantee that it controls that concept selectively.

Scenario

A research group investigates whether a language model represents sentiment in a relatively low-dimensional direction. The team collects hidden activations from:

Positive sentiment examples.

Negative sentiment examples.

It calculates the difference between their mean activations and uses this direction to modify model behavior. After intervention, the model produces more positive responses. The research team claims to have identified a causal sentiment direction. You are asked to investigate whether the intervention actually demonstrates selective control or merely introduces broader changes in the model's behavior.

Technical setup

At a chosen Transformer layer, let:

\[h^+\in\mathbb R^d\]

and:

\[h^-\in\mathbb R^d\]

represent activation samples from positive and negative sentiment examples. Define: \mathbb E[h^+], \qquad \mu_-= \mathbb E[h^-]. ] The steering direction is:

\[v=\ \frac{\mu+-\mu-}\ {|\mu+-\mu-|_2}.\]

Intervene on a residual representation:

\[h'=h+\alpha v,\]

where (\alpha) controls the intervention strength. For a simplified local analysis, define a target logit margin:

\[m(h)=w^\top h+b.\]

Research challenges

  • Explain how the difference of class-conditional means constructs a candidate sentiment direction.
  • Derive the exact change in the target logit margin under the linear approximation.
  • What happens when: \[w^\top v=0?\]
  • Explain why a direction derived from a difference of means may fail to isolate the intended semantic feature.
  • Construct a scenario in which positive and negative examples also differ in topic or sentence length. Explain how the resulting steering direction could capture these unintended correlations.
  • Compare mean-difference steering with a direction obtained using linear discriminant analysis.
  • Suppose the steering intervention is applied with increasing values of (\alpha). What would you measure to detect the point at which the intervention stops being selective?
  • Explain why excessive steering can move activations outside the model's commonly encountered activation region.
  • Design a control experiment using a randomly chosen direction with the same norm as (v).
  • Design another control using a direction orthogonal to (v) but with comparable activation magnitude.
  • How could steering one layer influence subsequent attention patterns and MLP activations?
  • Explain the distinction between changing an internal activation and establishing that the corresponding direction represents a single causal semantic feature.
  • Design an experiment measuring sentiment control alongside factual consistency, reasoning performance, style preservation, and unintended behavioral changes.

Hints

The difference of means identifies statistical separability, not necessarily a clean causal concept.

Measure both the intended behavioral change and the unrelated behaviors that may change simultaneously.

SET 15 / EXERCISE 09

Exercise 09 — Changing One Fact Inside a Language Model Without Retraining the Entire Model

Domain: Rank-one model editing · Factual memories · Locality and generalization

Core intuition: A targeted low-rank parameter update can modify a stored input-output association, but the geometric overlap between internal keys determines how much the edit interferes with other memories.

Scenario

A research laboratory discovers that its language model contains an outdated factual association. When asked about a specific scientific institution, the model returns an obsolete director. The company wants to update this fact without retraining billions of parameters. A researcher proposes editing the corresponding MLP transformation. The challenge is not just changing the intended association. It is preserving unrelated facts and avoiding collateral modifications.

Technical setup

Model the relevant MLP memory as:

\[v=Wk,\]

where:

(k\in\mathbb R^d) is an internal key representation.

(v\in\mathbb R^m) is the associated value.

(W\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}) is the relevant linear transformation.

Suppose the original association is:

\[Wk*=v{\mathrm{old}}.\]

The desired association is:

\[W'k*=v{\mathrm{new}}.\]

Define:

\[\Delta v=v{\mathrm{new}}-Wk*.\]

Consider the minimum-Frobenius-norm update satisfying the editing constraint:

\[\min_{\Delta W}|\Delta W|_F^2\]

subject to:

\[\Delta Wk_*=\Delta v.\]

Research challenges

  • Derive the minimum-norm rank-one update:
  • \frac{
  • \Delta v,k^\top
  • }{
  • |k|_2^2
  • }.
  • Verify directly that the update achieves the desired change at (k_*).
  • Show that the Frobenius norm of the update is:
  • \frac{|\Delta v|2}{|k*|_2}.
  • Suppose there is another factual association represented by key (k_j). Derive the change in its associated value: \[\Delta W k_j.\]
  • Express the collateral effect in terms of the cosine similarity between (k_*) and (k_j).
  • Explain why editing a key can unintentionally affect other facts whose internal representations point in similar directions.
  • Suppose there are (r) related contexts that must all receive the same new value. How would the editing problem change?
  • Discuss why one rank-one update might be insufficient when several desired contexts impose incompatible constraints.
  • Distinguish reliability of the edited factual answer from locality, which measures the preservation of unrelated behavior.
  • Design an evaluation using:
  • The requested factual prompt.
  • Paraphrases of the requested fact.
  • Related factual prompts.
  • Unrelated control prompts.
  • Explain how generalization testing can determine whether the model learned an actual updated association rather than memorizing one exact prompt.
  • Compare direct full-model fine-tuning, rank-one editing, and localized MLP editing.
  • Propose a release criterion balancing edit success, paraphrase generalization, locality, and preservation of previous capabilities.

Hints

The smallest update under the Frobenius norm is aligned with the input key direction.

The effect on another memory depends on how much its key overlaps with the edited key.

SET 15 / EXERCISE 10

Exercise 10 — The Attention Heads That Appear Useless Until You Remove All of Them

Domain: Circuit redundancy · Backup heads · Interventional ablation · Distributed computation

Core intuition: The absence of a large behavioral change after removing one component does not establish that the component is computationally irrelevant; several components may provide redundant or overlapping pathways.

Scenario

You investigate a Transformer that performs a particular syntactic operation. Your initial analysis identifies three attention heads that appear to contribute to the behavior. You remove the first head. The model continues performing almost identically. You remove the second head. The behavior still survives. You conclude that the two heads were probably irrelevant. However, when you remove the third head as well, the performance collapses. You suspect that the network has redundant computational pathways. You are asked to determine how individual and joint interventions reveal the structure of the underlying circuit.

Technical setup

Consider three head outputs:

\[h_1,h_2,h_3.\]

A simplified downstream computation is:

\[y=\ \mathbf1(h_1+h_2+h_3\geq1),\]

where each head produces a binary contribution:

\[h_i\in{0,1}.\]

For the intended task, all three heads produce:

\[h_1=h_2=h_3=1.\]

A head ablation sets its output to zero. This simplified model represents a thresholded downstream decision rather than a complete Transformer computation.

Research challenges

  • Calculate the original output.
  • Ablate each head individually and calculate the resulting output.
  • Ablate every pair of heads. Which combinations preserve the output?
  • Ablate all three heads. What happens?
  • Explain why individual ablation can fail to reveal a component's contribution when redundant pathways exist.
  • Distinguish exact redundancy from partial redundancy and compensatory behavior.
  • Suppose the downstream decision is instead based on: \[y= \ \sigma\left( \ 5(h_1+h_2+h_3)-7 \ \right).\]
  • Explain why removing one head may have a small effect on the final probability even though the underlying logit changes.
  • Why should researchers examine changes in internal margins and activation values rather than only measuring whether the final answer changes?
  • Design a systematic ablation experiment that examines all individual heads, pairs of heads, and the complete identified circuit.
  • Explain why removing several heads simultaneously can move the network into an activation regime that differs substantially from the distribution encountered during normal training.
  • Propose a method for distinguishing genuine backup circuits from components that merely respond to the same input feature.
  • Discuss the difference between a component being necessary for the original computation and a component being sufficient to reproduce the desired behavior.
  • Design an experiment that investigates whether remaining heads compensate after another head has been removed, rather than simply relying on pre-existing redundancy.

Hints

A component can make a real computational contribution without being individually necessary.

Evaluate combinations of interventions, not just isolated component removals.

End of Problem Set 15

Mechanistic interpretability research map

#

Research territory

Main capability

01 Induction heads Reconstructing algorithmic attention circuits

02 MLP key-value memories Understanding factual associations inside feed-forward layers

03 Direct logit attribution Decomposing prediction-relevant residual-stream contributions

04 Attention composition Investigating communication between attention heads

05 Feature superposition Separating latent features from individual neurons

06 Logit lens and tuned lens Tracking the development of predictions across layers

07 Attention sinks Understanding attention probability allocation and residual effects

08 Activation steering Investigating controllable directions in representation space

09 Rank-one model editing Modifying internal factual associations while preserving locality

10 Circuit redundancy Discovering backup pathways and distributed computations

Final examination standard

A complete solution should contain five elements.

  1. Mechanistic hypothesis

Identify the specific internal mechanism you believe explains the observed behavior.

  1. Mathematical reconstruction

Derive the relevant attention equations, activation transformations, residual contributions, and parameter updates.

  1. Causal investigation

Determine whether the proposed components actually influence the behavior rather than merely correlating with it.

  1. Alternative explanations

Identify other mechanisms that could produce the same observed behavior.

  1. Falsifiable experiment

Design an intervention or controlled evaluation that could prove your hypothesis wrong.

The ultimate challenge

Imagine you are given a pretrained Transformer with billions of parameters. You discover that it can:

Recognize repeated patterns.

Retrieve factual associations.

Perform indirect computations across attention heads.

Represent multiple semantic features within overlapping activation dimensions.

Develop predictions progressively through its layers.

Allocate attention to tokens that carry almost no semantic value.

Change behavior when a particular internal direction is modified.

Can you reconstruct these computations? Can you distinguish a feature from a neuron, a circuit from an individual head, a direct contribution from a causal contribution, and a correlation from an actual computational mechanism? And most importantly: Can you construct a falsifiable explanation of what the model is doing internally, rather than merely describing patterns that appear in its activations? That is the standard of mechanistic interpretability research.
